topics.title: Common chargers and USB-C
topics.subject: Science and Technology
topics.markdown:
## Core facts
- A common charging interface improves interoperability and reduces charger purchases and e-waste; USB-C identifies the connector, not a guarantee of identical charging speed.
- EU rules apply to specified rechargeable radio equipment from **28 December 2024**; laptops follow from **28 April 2026**. Covered categories include phones, tablets, cameras, headphones, handheld consoles, speakers, e-readers, keyboards, mice, navigation devices and earbuds. [EU Council](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/infographics/2022-06-07-common-charger-directive/).
## India and implementation
- The supplied January 2025 notes describe consultations beginning in 2022 and a proposed June 2025 phone/tablet deadline, followed by laptops in 2026. **Treat these Indian dates as source-reported proposals pending notification verification.**
- Benefits: reusable chargers, lower consumer costs, simpler inventories, less waste and easier international compatibility.
- Challenges: redesign costs, industry resistance, legacy devices, clear power-rating information and consumer awareness. Complement standardisation with repair, refurbishment and formal recycling.

topics.title: Coffee cultivation, heritage and exports
topics.subject: Indian Economy
topics.markdown:
## Idukki plantation history
- Pallikkunnu CSI Church near Kuttikkanam, Kerala, preserves an old coffee tree associated with colonial plantation history.
- Source account: British expansion in the early 19th century; coffee initially dominant around **Peerumade, Kuttikkanam and Thengakal**; leaf disease in **1875** encouraged a shift towards tea.
- The source reports a roughly 150-year-old tree and historical Thengakal yields of 2 tonnes/acre; these are local heritage claims requiring independent corroboration.
## Mains links
- Plantation economies show how disease, crop suitability and profitability reshape land use and livelihoods.
- Preserve agricultural heritage through cultural tourism; diversify crops and strengthen pest/climate resilience.
## Exports: January 2025 report
- **Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu** are major growing states; Karnataka leads. Europe is a key market: Italy, Belgium and Germany; other destinations include US, Russia and UAE.
- Higher Robusta prices and supply disruptions in Brazil/Vietnam can lift export value; distinguish price-driven receipts from volume growth. The source links pre-EUDR stockpiling to demand.
- Source's 'first ever $1 billion' claim and mixed April-November/FY labels are unreliable: official data show **$1.29 billion in FY2023-24**. [PIB coffee brief](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2025/jan/doc 2025120487201.pdf).
- **EUDR** means traceable deforestation-free supply chains; costs include documentation and monitoring. Avoid assuming every Indian exporter necessarily violates it or that the EU Foreign Subsidies Regulation applies uniformly to every coffee consignment.
- Mains: value-added exports, farmer incomes, diversification, climate/pest resilience, sustainable sourcing and trade compliance.

## Cultivation and Coffee Board
- Arabica/Robusta differ in environmental needs and product characteristics; Indian shade-grown coffee links production to tree cover but plantations do not automatically equal intact natural forest.
- Well-drained humus-rich soils, suitable rainfall/temperature and slope management matter; generic climate ranges are not universal specifications for both species.
- Baba Budan's introduction story is a historical tradition; source exact year should not be treated as conclusively established.
- **Coffee Act 1942; Coffee Board, Bengaluru**, 33 members. Chairperson and executive/Secretary roles should not be conflated.
- Source 65–70% export share is dated; contradictory production-rank lists should not be memorised. Quality, price volatility, pests, labour and climate resilience influence growers.

## Export update and production geography
- Source April–February **2024–25 export receipts: US$1.54 billion**, about 40% higher year on year. Revenue growth can reflect higher prices as well as quantities; it is not automatically a 40% production rise.
- Karnataka supplies roughly 70% of India's coffee; Kerala and Tamil Nadu are other major producers, with non-traditional areas including the Eastern Ghats.
- Shade cultivation, well-drained soils, rainfall and elevation matter; **Arabica and Robusta have different climatic tolerances**. Coffee rust is a fungal disease, not an insect pest.
- Source says more than two-thirds exported; destination shares/rankings require the same period. Brazil/Vietnam weather-related supply pressure can benefit receipts while global-price volatility remains a farmer risk.
- Coffee Board dates to **Coffee Act 1942**, Commerce Ministry. Do not infer a dedicated coffee PLI from a general manufacturing incentive, or an already operative India–EU FTA in March 2025.
- Value addition, speciality quality, resilient varieties, responsible shade management, market access and domestic demand support incomes; foreign-exchange earnings do not alone fix the current account.

## Araku Valley and tribal coffee
- **Eastern Ghats, Andhra Pradesh**, Araku landscape with **Anantagiri/Sunkarimetta forests**, hills including **Galikonda, Raktakonda, Sunkarimetta and Chitamogondi**. Source elevation **600–900 m** is a local range, not every surrounding hill's summit height; cooler highland conditions do not make the whole region a temperate climatic zone.
- **Araku Valley Arabica Coffee GI registered 2019**, official product name; GI protects qualifying geographic origin/reputation and use conditions, not a guarantee every bag is organic or sold by one commercial company. [GI Registry](https://search.ipindia.gov.in/GIRPublicSearch/Application/Details/607).
- Tribal farmers' coffee, forest produce and agriculture connect biodiversity, livelihoods and culture. “Araku tribes” is a geographical umbrella, not one named notified tribe; communities have distinct identities/knowledge.
- Cooperatives/social enterprises, suitable shade cultivation, processing and premium markets can improve incomes; measure farmer returns, control and certification rather than assume universal empowerment from branding.
- Bauxite **deposits/mining proposals and ecological conflict** must be separated from proof the whole valley is an operating mine. Forest/water protection, recognised land/community rights and meaningful consultation matter.
- Tourism nickname **“Ooty of Andhra Pradesh”** reflects scenic appeal, not scientific geography. Ecotourism/agro-tourism require carrying-capacity, waste/water management and community benefit sharing; scenic promotion alone is not sustainable development.

topics.title: Manufactured sand
topics.subject: Environment
topics.markdown:
## Meaning and policy context
- **M-sand**: sand-size aggregate produced by crushing suitable rock, including granite/basalt, often using a **Vertical Shaft Impact (VSI)** crusher.
- Source context: Rajasthan M-Sand Policy 2024 seeks to reduce dependence on river sand and encourage sustainable construction.
## Benefits and limits
- Reduces riverbed disturbance, erosion, groundwater impacts and habitat damage from excessive extraction.
- Controlled processing can improve grading and consistent supply; suitable mine overburden may provide feedstock after quality testing.
- Cost and construction performance depend on rock quality, processing and transport. **Do not memorise the source's blanket claim that M-sand needs no washing:** fines removal and treatment may be necessary.
## Way forward
- Enforce grading/quality standards; invest in local processing and logistics; offer appropriate incentives and research support; demonstrate performance to builders; support alternative livelihoods for affected mining workers.

topics.title: E-waste and extended producer responsibility
topics.subject: Environment
topics.markdown:
## Core facts
- E-waste is discarded electrical/electronic equipment. Hazardous constituents include **lead, mercury, cadmium, chromium and beryllium**.
- **EPR** shifts end-of-life responsibility towards producers; collection, authorised recycling and certificate systems help implement obligations.
- The source reports 2024 amendments enabling EPR-certificate trading; verify the applicable category and target rather than assuming a uniform 25% recycling obligation.
## January 2025 source figures
- Generation: **1.751 million tonnes in 2023-24**, reported increase **72.54%**; recycled share **43%**, untreated share **57%**. The comparison year and statistical definitions need verification.
- Source also cites 65 cities generating 60% and 10 states generating 70%; baseline years are unspecified.
## Risks and response
- Unsafe informal dismantling/burning contaminates air, soil and water and exposes workers. Landfilling can leach toxins; uncontrolled incineration releases hazardous emissions.
- Priorities: take-back points, authorised recyclers, worker training and formalisation, repair/reuse/refurbishment, better recovery technology, public awareness and enforcement.
- **Basel Convention**: hazardous-waste transboundary movement; **Minamata Convention**: mercury. Domestic links include hazardous-waste regulation and circular-economy policy.
## PYQ trap
- UPSC Prelims 2013: beryllium, cadmium, chromium, mercury and lead are the relevant listed substances; answer **(b)**. The full question is in the common Environment PYQ file.
- PYQ recall: **EPR was an important feature of the e-Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011**; distinguish the historical rule asked in 2019 from later replacement rules.

## May 2025: certificate pricing and reliable measurement
- **E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022** took effect **1 April 2023**; producer obligations are implemented through registered actors, recycling targets and **EPR certificates** on CPCB's portal. Certificate compliance must reflect actual recycling/recovery, not fictitious transactions. [CPCB portal and rules](https://eprewaste.cpcb.gov.in/).
- **2024 amendments** provide certificate exchange-price bands linked to environmental compensation: floor **30%**, ceiling **100%** of applicable compensation. This is not a single rupee price for every device, nor a floor-price provision that should be attributed solely to the original 2022 text. Follow applicable CPCB methodology/date; later August 2025 guidelines are not proof of the exact May price table.
- Predictable remuneration can support collection, transport and verified recovery investments. Producers' cost/pass-through concerns require assessment against environmental/health externalities; pricing without audits/traceability can still produce paper compliance.
- Source compares **708,445 tonnes (2017–18)** with **1,778,400 (2023–24)**, claims **151.03%** growth and **169,283 tonnes/year** increase. These are source figures with unresolved classification comparability and arithmetic: the endpoint increase is about **151.0%**, average over six year-to-year intervals about **178,326 tonnes/year**, not the printed annual figure.
- Reject unsupported universal claims of informal workers' **lifespan below 27 years**. The source's **95% informal share**, **<10% formal versus 70%+ EU**, **₹80,000 crore / US$10bn / US$20bn / US$20bn** loss estimates lack harmonised years/definitions and cannot be added or treated as established national totals.
- Unsafe acid extraction/burning exposes workers, including women/children, to toxic substances and contaminates soil/water/air. Recover gold/copper and other materials through authorised technology; encourage durable/modular products, repair/refurbishment, state-level material tracking and recovery-based incentives.
- Integrate informal collectors through training, safe jobs and fair payment rather than abrupt livelihood exclusion; strengthen recycler verification, take-back access, public awareness and health protections.

## June 2025: silver recovery using fatty acids
- Research by Helsinki/Jyväskylä scientists explores **oleic, linoleic and linolenic acids plus aqueous hydrogen peroxide** for dissolving/recovering silver under mild conditions. This is a controlled chemical process, not simply adding cooking oil to scrap. [Original research](https://helda.helsinki.fi/server/api/core/bitstreams/6370fbb8-1b67-42dd-82d3-bb5a300fea40/content).
- Silver's electrical conductivity supports electronics, photovoltaic contacts and vehicle components; photovoltaics' semiconductor absorbs light, while silver contacts carry current.
- **Urban mining** recovers secondary materials from discarded products; it differs from extracting virgin urban mineral deposits. Safer solvents may reduce burdens of cyanide/strong-acid routes, but scale, selectivity, reagent recovery, cost and worker protection need assessment.
- June source's per-device silver quantities and recovery percentage are indicative estimates with unspecified product/year coverage; they are not a universal inventory or proof that all unrecovered silver is permanently lost.

topics.title: Operation Greens
topics.subject: Indian Economy
topics.markdown:
## Purpose and scope
- Launched **2018** by the **Ministry of Food Processing Industries**: improve producer returns, stabilise prices for producers/consumers, reduce post-harvest losses and build processing capacity.
- Initially **TOP = Tomato, Onion, Potato**. Budget 2021-22 expanded long-term coverage to **22 perishables, including shrimp**. [MoFPI/PIB](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleaseIframePage.aspx?PRID=1744337&lang=2&reg=48).
- Supports value-chain infrastructure, farmer-producer organisations, storage, transport, processing and cluster-to-market links; short-term support and long-term projects should be distinguished.
## Parliamentary review reported in January 2025
- Source reports **34% of Rs 59.44 crore** allocated for 2024-25 spent by October 2024, alongside Maharashtra onion-price falls and potato shortages. Preserve the reporting period; do not present these as current figures.
- Bottlenecks: unused funds, inadequate cold chains, stakeholder coordination, export-policy uncertainty and weather/supply shocks.
## Mains framework
- Producer income + consumer affordability require predictable trade decisions, timely funding, market intelligence, efficient logistics and accountable implementation.

topics.title: Lead pollution and public health
topics.subject: Environment
topics.markdown:
## Exposure and effects
- Lead is a toxic metal; exposure comes from unsafe battery recycling, paints, contaminated products, occupational dust and legacy pollution. Geological weathering is a natural source.
- Children are especially vulnerable: impaired brain development, learning and behaviour; other effects include anaemia, kidney damage, hypertension and reproductive harm.
- **No known safe blood lead level.** A 5 micrograms/dL action threshold is not a safety boundary. [WHO guidance](https://www.who.int/news/item/27-10-2021-who-guidance-to-reduce-illness-due-to-lead-exposure).
- India phased out leaded petrol by 2000, but contamination can persist.
## Regulation and response
- **Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022** replaced the **Batteries (Management and Handling) Rules, 2001**. They cover multiple battery categories and use EPR for collection/recycling/refurbishment. The source's title 'Lead Battery Waste Management Rules (2016)' is incorrect. [MoEFCC/PIB](https://www.pib.gov.in/Pressreleaseshare.aspx?PRID=1854433&lang=2&reg=48).
- Priorities: safer products, formal recycling, occupational protection, child/pregnancy screening, pollution monitoring/remediation and reliable exposure data.
## Source figures requiring baseline checks
- January 2025 PDFs cite 275 million exposed children, 4.6 million DALYs and 165,000 annual deaths, but omit the underlying study years/thresholds.
- They identify Bihar, UP, MP, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Andhra Pradesh as high-burden states and cite a 40% share with unclear denominator. Keep these as unverified source estimates, not a definitive state ranking.

topics.title: Sea-level rise and coastal adaptation
topics.subject: Environment
topics.markdown:
## Causes and consequences
- Ocean warming causes **thermal expansion**; melting **land ice** adds ocean water. Ocean circulation and land subsidence/uplift affect regional relative sea level.
- Impacts: inundation, erosion, saltwater intrusion, freshwater/crop damage, displacement, waterborne disease and fishing/tourism losses.
- Indian examples: Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata, Sundarbans mangroves and Odisha's olive-ridley nesting beaches.
## Adaptation
- Risk-sensitive coastal zoning/CRZ enforcement; early warnings and evacuation; climate-resilient infrastructure; mangrove restoration; context-appropriate protection and managed retreat; saline-tolerant agriculture.
## Climate target distinction
- India's 2022 updated NDC aimed for about **50% of cumulative installed electric-power capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030**. This is not 50% of all energy use or necessarily of electricity generation. [Official NDC explanation](https://www.pib.gov.in/Pressreleaseshare.aspx?PRID=1913467&lang=2&reg=48).
## Quantitative caution
- Source estimates (~20 cm rise since 1880, rate increasing from ~2 to ~4 mm/year, 1.2 m by 2100, 80% Sundarbans loss) lack consistent periods/scenarios. Do not treat them as universal forecasts; retain in fact-review pending underlying evidence.
- The source's 30% EV-share goal also needs its policy scope verified.

## Coastal displacement and labour rights
- **Satabhaya, Odisha** illustrates why relocation requires livelihoods, freshwater, housing and services as well as new land. Ports, aquaculture and energy infrastructure can compound mangrove/estuary degradation and restrict customary coastal access; project-specific impacts require assessment.
- Displaced fishing/farming households may enter urban construction, brick kilns or domestic work with debt bondage, insecure housing and gendered exploitation. India lacks a dedicated comprehensive climate-displacement framework, but **Article 21, disaster management, environmental/coastal regulation and labour protections** remain relevant.
- Community examples in the article: **Ennore Creek protests, Tamil Nadu; Pattuvam mangrove protection, Kerala; Save Satabhaya, Odisha**. Rights-based adaptation should include participation, fair compensation, decent employment and protection from trafficking/forced labour.
- **SDG 8.7** concerns forced labour, modern slavery, trafficking and child labour; **8.5** concerns full productive employment and decent work. The source merges these targets.

topics.title: Tamu Lhosar
topics.subject: Indian Art and Culture
topics.markdown:
## Identification
- **Gurung community**, predominantly Nepal: New Year celebration; **Tamu** refers to Gurung people and **Lhosar** to New Year.
- Observed on **15 Poush** (late December); festivities include feasts, dances, music and ethnic dress.
- Associated districts: Lamjung, Gorkha, Tanahun, Syangja, Manang, Kaski and Parbat; Kathmandu's Tundikhel hosts celebrations, but the festival is not exclusive to the capital.
- Source dress terms: women - Makhamali blouse/Ghalek shawl; men - Bhoto/Bhangra/Kachhad.
## Significance and exam trap
- Cultural continuity, community identity, intergenerational transmission and tourism; Nepal recognises the festival as a holiday.
- **Do not equate 15 Poush with the astronomical winter solstice.** The supplied practice question incorrectly treats the solstice claim as true.

topics.title: Manufacturing, Make in India and PLI
topics.subject: Indian Economy
topics.markdown:
## Policy framework
- **Make in India (2014)**: investment, manufacturing capability and employment.
- **PLI (introduced 2020)**: incentives linked to eligible incremental production/sales; coverage expanded across **14 sectors**. Defence and toys are not automatically PLI-covered merely because domestic manufacturing is promoted.
- Supporting levers: industrial corridors, logistics parks, National Infrastructure Pipeline, skills, infrastructure and business reforms.
## January 2025 source claims
- PDFs report Rs 1.28 lakh crore investment and 8.5 lakh jobs, mobile-phone production +600% and toy exports +239%; the measurement windows are unspecified, so use only after baseline verification.
## Opportunities and constraints
- Electronics, pharmaceuticals, renewable-energy equipment and defence; supply-chain diversification after COVID-19 can attract investment.
- Challenges: logistics, skills, technology, predictable regulation, environmental compliance and competition from Vietnam/Bangladesh.
- **India did not join RCEP in November 2019.** The source's claim that RCEP participation strengthened India's manufacturing position is wrong. [Commerce Ministry/PIB](https://www.pib.gov.in/newsite/PrintRelease.aspx?lang=2&reg=48&relid=200213).
## Mains approach
- Combine productivity and scale with jobs, domestic supplier capacity, resilient trade links and sustainable production.
## Specialty steel: PLI 1.1
- Launched **6 January 2025**, second round; production period **FY 2025–26 to 2029–30**. First specialty-steel round notified **29 July 2021**, within the broader PLI initiative begun in 2020.
- Five categories: **coated/plated steel; high-strength/wear-resistant steel; specialty rails; alloy steel and wires; electrical steel**. Uses: automobiles, white goods, transformers and specialised industries.
- Changes: lower **CRGO** investment/capacity thresholds; excess production carried forward to the **immediately following year** for incentive eligibility; augmentation of existing mills eligible; quality/energy efficiency/process improvement.
- **Cold-Rolled Grain-Oriented steel**: transformer cores, high-tension power distribution; January 2025 ministry says domestic technology gap. Do not treat this as a timeless 'no Indian producer' claim.
- **PLI rewards eligible production, not simply any steel investment**. [Ministry release](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2090683&lang=2&reg=48).

## Andhra Pradesh project map: January 2025
- Projects announced/inaugurated/foundation stones at Visakhapatnam worth **over ₹2 lakh crore** include clean energy, railways and manufacturing; not all are completed factories.
- **South Coast Railway headquarters, Visakhapatnam**: regional rail administration/connectivity.
- **Bulk Drug Park, Nakkapalli, Anakapalli district**, near **Visakhapatnam–Chennai Industrial Corridor**; APIs/pharmaceutical supply chains and reduced import dependence.
- **Krishnapatnam Industrial Area / KRIS City**, **Chennai–Bengaluru Industrial Corridor**; source **₹10,500 crore**, potential **~1 lakh jobs**; greenfield smart industrial development under **National Industrial Corridor Development Programme**.
- Evaluate land/clearance, water/power, logistics, skills, local benefits and ecological compliance; expected jobs are projections.

## May 2025 editorial: innovation-led manufacturing reset
- D. N. Gupta argues technical education, **core engineering/R&D** and production ecosystems matter alongside industrial incentives and shifting US tariffs. Liberalisation **1991**, **National Manufacturing Competitiveness Programme 2005**, Make in India 2014 are milestones; India's manufacturing efforts predate 1991.
- Source 2023 comparisons: manufacturing value added **India US$461bn, China US$4,658bn, US US$2,497bn**; per-capita **India ~US$320/world ~US$2,000**, productivity **India ~US$8,900/world ~US$32,000**. These are dated article indicators with methodology/price bases not fully given; per-worker productivity, per-capita value added and aggregate size differ, and they are not 2025 results.
- Reform entrance assessments/curricula towards concepts, creativity, problem-solving, collaboration and applied research; grades are useful but insufficient. Proposed **50% practical work** requires labs, tool rooms, workshops, assembly facilities and trained mentors—an editorial recommendation, not a mandatory national rule.
- Build **civil/mechanical/electrical/chemical/textile/biotech** capacity alongside AI/IT and electronics; equipment/machinery/process design underpin physical production. Avoid assuming service-startup growth supplies every manufacturing capability.
- State-specific parks with plug-and-play infrastructure, common prototyping/testing/certification/design, links to institutions/labs and supplier/startup finance. Lessons from Silicon Valley concern skills, research and networks, not a promise one copied park creates equivalent outcomes.
- Proposed **R&D 0.65%→2% GDP** and **additional 1% GDP industrial infrastructure** are spending recommendations; reference-year/scope of the 0.65% baseline must be specified. Combine educational capability, affordable finance, scale/quality, market access and dynamic evidence-based policy; check productivity/jobs and domestic technological depth.

## June clipping: PLI performance
- Newspaper reports **₹21,534 crore incentives disbursed** across sectors, investment **₹1.76 lakh crore** and production/sales **₹16.5 lakh crore**. The clipping dates production/sales to **March**; these cumulative administrative figures have different measures, so keep them distinct from annual output, net value addition or attributable employment.
- Source's smartphone **FY2017–18 imports US$3.6bn/exports US$0.334bn → FY2022–23 imports US$1.6bn/exports US$11bn** describes a shift toward net exports; its stated **US$9.8bn surplus is arithmetically inconsistent** with those rounded latter numbers (**US$9.4bn**). Do not use the pre-PLI baseline as proof every gain was caused solely by PLI.
- **2023 export-share/PLI PYQ: (d)**—3.2% share of global goods exports is incorrect in the question's context; domestic and foreign firms can use eligible PLI schemes. Sector-specific base-year/eligibility rules mean incentives are not universally calculated against the immediately preceding year's sales.

topics.title: Defence manufacturing and exports
topics.subject: Internal Security of India
topics.markdown:
## Dated figures and targets
- FY2023-24 exports: **Rs 21, 083 crore**, source reports **32.5% annual growth**, private sector 60% / DPSUs 40%.
- FY2024-25 defence allocation reported: **Rs 6.22 lakh crore**. Source production figures: Rs 74, 054 crore (2016-17) to Rs 108, 684 crore (2022-23), with 21.96% private share in the latter year.
- Export ambition: **Rs 50, 000 crore by 2028-29/2029**. Keep a target separate from an achieved outcome.
- Care Edge forecast cited: sector growth 20% CAGR and exports 19% CAGR over FY24-FY29; these are projections, not observed growth.
## Drivers and constraints
- Indigenisation, procurement demand, export facilitation, technology transfer and startups; benefits include strategic autonomy, employment and technology spillovers.
- Constraints: critical subsystem/design gaps, R&D and finance, coordination, certification, long procurement cycles and dependence on imported technologies.
## Policy and strategy
- FDI: source cites 74% automatic route and up to 100% government route subject to applicable conditions; defence corridors in **UP and Tamil Nadu**; Strategic Partnership Model and export-promotion support.
- Do not memorise the source's defence **TUFS** claim without verification: TUFS is associated with textiles. The alleged 60% import share/startup count also lacks a clear baseline.
- Modern warfare requires cyber/AI/space skills, joint-service training and multi-domain readiness; defence attachés support military diplomacy. **Army War College: Mhow.**
## Mains answer plan
- Security need → domestic capability and exports → technology/finance gaps → predictable procurement, R&D, supplier development and jointness.
## Aero-engines: January 2025 development debate
- DRDO chief **Samir V. Kamat** called for foreign co-development of advanced engines; source describes demonstrated fourth-generation engine technologies and a future **sixth-generation ambition**, not an operational Indian sixth-generation engine.
- Desired **thrust-to-weight ratio above 10**, high-temperature **single-crystal turbine blades**, **powder-metallurgy discs**, **ceramic-matrix composites**; lighter, heat-resistant components improve efficiency/performance.
- Engine 'generation' terminology is not a universal substitute for fighter-aircraft generation; materials demonstrated are not proof a complete certified engine is ready.
- Test/manufacturing gaps: **high-altitude facility, flying test bed, large forging capacity**, source **50, 000-tonne press**, skilled workforce and certification.
- Source investment proposal **₹40, 000–50, 000 crore**, approximate **$4–5 billion**; research share **5% → suggested 15% of defence budget** is an argument, not a notified requirement. Unspecified cross-country R&D percentages are not comparable verified series.
- **Safran (France), Rolls-Royce (UK), GE (USA)** cited as potential partners; discussion does not mean all proposed contracts signed.
- Benefits: autonomy, potential exports/jobs and spillovers to civil aviation, space and materials. Risks: IP/technology-transfer restrictions, dependence, delays and cost. Evaluate actual design access, domestic capability and certification milestones.

## Him Kavach: cold-weather protection, January 2025
- DRDO **modular multi-layer clothing system**, reported to have cleared user trials; designed temperature range **+20°C to −60°C**, rugged/all-weather operation.
- Add/remove insulating layers; breathability and moisture management maintain comfort. Passive insulation **retains body heat**, not proof the clothing actively generates warmth.
- Earlier **ECWCS**, Extreme Cold Weather Clothing System, associated with **DIPAS**, three-layer protection; source's blanket claim it fails in all Siachen conditions is overstated.
- Trials/design range are not a guarantee of zero cold injury or proof universal troop rollout; exposure, fit, activity, shelter and acclimatisation still matter.

## Trajan: January 2025 export report
- **Larsen & Toubro + France's KNDS**, **155 mm / 52-calibre towed artillery**; reported **Armenian order**, not proof every component is Indian-origin.
- Indigenous components include auxiliary power unit, control panel and rolling gear assembly. Range **over 40 km**, ammunition-dependent; modular mobility, loading/fire-control assistance and varied-terrain deployment.
- **Towed gun ≠ self-propelled howitzer**; barrel calibre designation differs from bore diameter. Export prospects depend on orders, delivery, spares/training and technology cooperation.

## T-72 bridge-laying tanks: 21 January 2025 contract
- **47 BLTs**, **Heavy Vehicles Factory, Armoured Vehicle Nigam Limited**, **₹1, 560.52 crore** (source rounded **₹1, 561 crore**), **Buy (Indian-IDDM)** procurement. [Defence Ministry](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleaseIframePage.aspx?PRID=2094857&lang=2&reg=48).
- Mechanised formation **bridging obstacles** during offensive/defensive movement; bridge-laying support vehicle differs from a tank firing its main gun. Mobility, indigenous manufacture, jobs and reliable lifecycle support are the policy links.

## Aero India 2025
- **15 th edition, 10–14 February, Yelahanka, Bengaluru**; source **931 exhibitors / 150 foreign companies / around 90 participating countries** are event figures, not continuing industry totals.
- Su-57 and F-35 display, LCA/AMCA projects, **BRIDGE Defence Ministers' Conclave**, CEO roundtable and **i DEX** promote defence diplomacy, start-ups/MSMEs, supply chains and investment.
- Source **₹1.27 lakh crore production / ~₹21, 000 crore exports** refer to earlier reported annual performance; **₹1.60 lakh crore / ₹30, 000 crore** figures are projections, not then-achieved FY2025–26 outcomes.
- Jet-engine dependence, procurement delays, skills and IP/technology transfer remain constraints. Exhibition participation is not a procurement commitment; “Tejas production stabilised” should not erase delivery/engine bottlenecks.

## Export figures: denominator traps
- February repeat cites **28% historical export CAGR /19% forecast to FY29**; different periods and projections must remain separate.
- **Myanmar 31% /Sri Lanka 19%** are not a verified current breakdown of every defence-export item; recipient shares vary with year, data and equipment coverage.
- Source says defence budget both **1.9–2.8%** and **3%GDP /60% imports** without matching scope; don't memorise them as one consistent series.
- **Tamil Nadu/UP corridors, FDI subject to conditions, strategic partnerships, export facilitation, i DEX/R&D** matter; the alleged defence TUFS programme confuses textile policy, and a draft promotion policy is not automatically operational.
- Improve competitive products, certification, delivery/spares, finance and end-use compliance; domestic procurement preference alone cannot create global demand.

## 29 May 2025: delivery discipline and design
- At the **CII Annual Business Summit**, Air Chief Marshal **A. P. Singh** criticised unrealistic contract commitments and project delays, urged private industry's contribution and stressed indigenous **design/development**, not assembly alone. His emphatic delay remarks are a speaker's assessment, not an audited demonstration that every Indian defence project missed its deadline.
- **27 May:** Defence Minister approved the **AMCA Programme Execution Model**. **ADA** will execute with an Indian industry partner chosen through competition; private and public sectors receive opportunities. Approval of the model is not proof a private partner was selected, aircraft produced or fighter entered service. [Defence Ministry](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2131528&lang=1&reg=6).
- His praise of Operation Sindoor concerns operational performance; the speech does not establish a new combat event on 29 May. Existing Operation Sindoor notes retain chronology and attribution.
- Capability requires design/IP, prototype testing, certification, supply chains, skilled staff and predictable orders; production capacity alone is not frontier technology. Low output, uncertain returns and service-industry trust can inhibit scale.
- Improve realistic milestones, procurement decisions, accountable delivery, prototype/R&D support and competitive partnerships. The current capital procurement framework is **Defence Acquisition Procedure 2020**; source's generic DPP reference should not be treated as the latest named instrument. Proposed incentives/PPPs are recommendations rather than accomplished reforms.
- Practice answer: delayed delivery → preparedness gap → technology/contract/capacity constraints → credible milestones, competition, design capability and lifecycle support.

## June 2025 speech and source corrections
- Clipping repeats **Defence Minister Rajnath Singh's ₹50,000-crore exports by 2029 goal** at **IIT Mandi's 16th Foundation Day**; it is a speech report, not exports already achieved or necessarily a newly announced June target. Its **~88% ammunition self-sufficiency** is a speaker/source figure requiring category/year, not all defence equipment self-sufficiency.
- Official FY2024–25 exports **₹23,622 crore** is distinct from prose's recycled FY2023–24 figures and forecasts. **CareEdge 20% production /19% export CAGR through FY2029** remain forecasts; source's 28% historical CAGR needs its stated period. [Defence export brief](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2025/apr/doc202543531401.pdf).
- Existing notes retain the denominator cautions for Myanmar/Sri Lanka recipient shares, private/DPSU shares, budget/GDP and import spending, and correct the misattributed defence **TUFS**.
- June prose also mislabels administration as “Ministry of Industrial Promotion” and presents an “India Defence Mart” export-licensing portal/universal defence EPC without verified legal identity. Use actual **MoD/DDP export-authorisation mechanisms, Defence Exports Promotion Scheme**, industrial corridors and applicable investment/procurement policies; do not invent a newly operational agency from generic names.
- Proposed Green Channel expansion and advanced-system/startup support are suggestions; **194 startups** is an undated source snapshot, not India's complete current ecosystem. Private share of exports does not equal private share of all production/procurement.
- Mains: predictable procurement and finance, design/R&D, export certification, reliable delivery/spares, partnerships and end-use compliance; targets and exhibition participation do not establish actual sales or complete technology autonomy.

## DAC: 3 July 2025
- **Acceptance of Necessity ≈₹1.05 lakh crore, 10 capital proposals, Buy (Indian-IDDM)**: armoured recovery vehicles, electronic warfare, tri-services common inventory management, SAMs, moored mines, mine countermeasure vessels, super-rapid gun mounts and submersible autonomous vessels.
- Mobility, air defence, logistics and maritime safety are intended benefits. **AoN ≠ signed contract ≠ delivery**; the indigenous category requires applicable design/development/manufacture criteria. [MoD](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleaseIframePage.aspx?PRID=2141835&lang=2&reg=48).

topics.title: Citizenship, visas and deportation
topics.subject: Indian Polity
topics.markdown:
## Constitutional and statutory distinction
- **Part II, Articles 5-11** addresses citizenship at commencement and Parliament's power to legislate; it does not itself prescribe all present-day acquisition procedures.
- **Citizenship Act, 1955** governs birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory; loss through renunciation, termination or deprivation.
- Citizenship is a Union subject; **CAA 2019** provides a special route for specified Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi and Christian migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan entering by **31 December 2014**, subject to statutory conditions/exemptions. It is not automatic citizenship for every such entrant.
## MHA annual report 2023-24: source figures
- FRRO deportations **2, 331**: Nigeria 1, 470; Bangladesh 411; Uganda 78; reasons include visa violations/overstay.
- **1, 112** long-term visas to Pakistani minority-community members; LTV is not citizenship.
- Citizenship certificates **1, 699**: registration **1, 278** + naturalisation **421**; this source table excludes CAA figures.
- Foreign visitors **98 lakh**: Bangladesh 21.1 lakh, US 17.4 lakh, UK 9.9 lakh.
- Source lists Amendment Act years 1986, 1992, 2003, 2005, 2015, 2019; avoid turning this source list into an assertion that no other changes exist.
## NRI, PIO and OCI: diaspora distinction
| Term | Citizenship / meaning |
| --- | --- |
| NRI | Indian citizen residing abroad; residence definitions depend on the law/context |
| PIO | Person of Indian origin; historical/demographic description can continue |
| OCI cardholder | Eligible **foreign national**, registered under Citizenship Act, 1955 **section 7A**; not an Indian citizen |
- **PIO card scheme merged into OCI in 2015**; the demographic category 'person of Indian origin' was not abolished.
- Eligibility connects to qualifying Indian citizenship/territory and descendants, subject to statutory conditions; Pakistan/Bangladesh citizenship/ancestry exclusions apply as prescribed. Do not infer eligibility from Indian ethnicity alone.
- OCI is **not dual citizenship**. No Indian voting rights, election eligibility or ordinary entitlement to constitutional/public posts; visa/residence privileges and permitted activities remain subject to rules. [MHA explanation](https://www.mha.gov.in/PDF_Other/1OCIcardholder_Introduction_15112019.pdf), [OCI FAQ](https://ociservices.gov.in/onlineOCI/onlineOCI/faq).

## US birthright citizenship: January 2025 clipping
- **20 January executive order** sought to restrict recognition for specified US-born children of non-citizen parents; State litigation immediately followed, invoking **14th Amendment** protection.
- An executive announcement is not proof constitutional birthright citizenship was finally abolished. **Birth citizenship ≠ H-1B employment permission ≠ green-card status**; Indian citizenship rules must be assessed separately.

- EO targeted specified children whose mother was unlawfully present or lawfully temporary and father neither US citizen nor lawful permanent resident, prospectively after a 30-day period; parental tests are more specific than “all foreign parents”. [20 January order](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/protecting-the-meaning-and-value-of-american-citizenship/).

## US deportations: February 2025
- **5 February 2025:** US military flight brought **104 Indians to Amritsar**, correcting the PDF's preliminary “around 200”. Nationality verification and acceptance of own citizens differ from endorsing detention/transport conditions. [Contemporaneous report](https://apnews.com/article/eb 43d 6fb 6ba 1f 78febdd 78b 77bd 36196).
- Source **18, 000** refers to a reported removal/enforcement population; not a census of all undocumented Indians in the US. Legal students/workers are not automatically undocumented migrants.
- Balance sovereign immigration enforcement with due process, dignity, humane treatment, consular assistance and protection against trafficking; reintegration needs counselling, skills/jobs and action against fraudulent agents.
- **Trump**, not Biden, was US President for this February 2025 sequence; Modi's impending visit was a diplomatic context, not proof of a settled deportation agreement.

## Irregular migration and rights
- Irregular entry/overstay, refugee protection, smuggling and trafficking are different categories; trafficking centres on exploitation and need not involve crossing a border.
- Article 21 protects persons, including non-citizens; immigration enforcement must respect applicable law and due process. CAA exceptions have specified conditions, not a general exemption for all migrants.
- Drivers include work, persecution, disasters and family networks. Recruitment regulation/eMigrate, safe-migration training, consular support and border management need coordination.
- Migration agreements do not eliminate domestic unemployment or guarantee every applicant an overseas job; source agent counts are dated.

## Immigration and Foreigners Bill: March 2025
- Introduced on 11 March 2025; introduction is distinct from passage, assent and commencement.
- Proposed consolidation of **Passport (Entry into India) Act 1920; Registration of Foreigners Act 1939; Foreigners Act 1946; Immigration (Carriers' Liability) Act 2000**. It did not repeal the Citizenship Act 1955 or Passports Act 1967. [Official account](https://www.pib.gov.in/Pressreleaseshare.aspx?PRID=2115972&lang=2&reg=48).
- Covers entry, exit, stay, travel documents, carrier information and reporting by institutions accommodating foreigners. Registration depends on visa/category conditions, not a universal rule for every visitor.
- Proposed undocumented-entry penalty: up to five years and ₹5 lakh; forged documents: two to seven years and ₹1–10 lakh. These are Bill provisions in this dated update.
- Articles 14 and 21 protect persons; Article 19 rights are for citizens. National security and public health controls must coexist with due process, proportionality and constitutional judicial review.
- Assess compliance costs, privacy, clear procedures and business/student mobility alongside security objectives.

## May 2025: detention and the rule of law
- Assam's final **2019 NRC excluded roughly 19 lakh people**; the PDF wrongly equates exclusion with citizenship being stripped. **Non-inclusion alone does not declare someone a foreigner**; tribunal/legal process is distinct. [MHA clarification](https://www.mha.gov.in/sites/default/files/PressRelease_NRC_20082019.pdf).
- Assam citizenship verification involved the **24 March 1971 midnight cutoff** and proof/ancestry questions; floods, missing records and spelling differences can impede fair adjudication. Avoid treating every excluded person as detained or stateless.
- Source cites **Foreigners Act 1946** detention/deportation powers and **NSA 1980** preventive detention. These are different legal grounds, not interchangeable authority to hold all non-citizens indefinitely. Assent to the Immigration and Foreigners Act 2025 did not alone commence its replacement framework.
- **Article 21 protects persons**. Article 22's arrest/preventive-detention provisions have exceptions and safeguards; all clauses do not apply identically to every detention category. Courts can review legality, purpose, fairness and proportionality.
## Editorial critique and comparative judgment
- Source invokes **Rajubala Das v Union of India**, identified with a 2020 proceeding; do not treat that year as a verified final judgment or assume all requested relief was granted.
- **NZYQ (Australia, 2023)**: continued immigration detention lacked constitutional justification where no real prospect of removal becoming practicable in the reasonably foreseeable future existed. This concerns Australia's constitutional separation of powers, not an automatically binding Indian rule. [High Court summary](https://www.hcourt.gov.au/sites/default/files/assets/publications/judgment-summaries/2023/hca-37-2023-11-28.pdf).
- Source's **26 deported (2017–2023)/over 1.5 lakh declared foreigners** is an editorial dataset claim with unclear matching cohorts; it does not establish the status of every detainee. Feasibility of receiving-country acceptance and nationality verification matters.
- Policy argument: detention needs a lawful purpose, individual assessment, periodic review, fair hearings/legal aid and humane conditions; evaluate alternatives when removal is unrealistic. The editorial's blanket unlawfulness claim should not replace case-specific legal findings.

## 8 May 2025 hearing: Rohingya and UNHCR cards
- Embedded clipping reports Supreme Court oral observations that persons determined to be foreigners could be dealt with under applicable law, including deportation following prescribed procedure. Petitioners invoked **non-refoulement**, feared persecution in Myanmar and alleged removal of persons holding UNHCR cards; these are litigating claims, not facts conclusively adjudicated by the clipping.
- **Articles 14 and 21** protect persons; citizen-specific **Article 19(1)(e)** residence/settlement rights differ. A UNHCR card does not itself confer Indian citizenship or an unconditional statutory right to remain.
- The Court scheduled fuller hearing for **July**. Distinguish oral/interim observations, existing executive powers under the then-applicable Foreigners Act, and a final determination of the pending refugee-protection claims; India's non-membership of the Refugee Convention does not answer every constitutional/procedural question.

topics.title: Similipal and tiger conservation
topics.subject: Environment
topics.markdown:
## Similipal
- **Mayurbhanj, Odisha**; associated elephant-reserve landscape includes Hadgarh and Kuldiha sanctuaries. Named for red silk-cotton trees.
- Forests: moist mixed deciduous, semi-evergreen and dry deciduous with grasslands; rivers **Khairi and Deo**; elephants, carnivores and mugger crocodiles.
- UNESCO World Network of Biosphere Reserves since **2009**; notable wild **pseudo-melanistic tigers**. Avoid the source's unsupported 'Asia's second-largest biosphere' ranking and any confusion between biosphere reserve, national park and tiger-reserve boundaries.
## Tiger basics
- National animal; **keystone/predator** and ecosystem-health indicator; IUCN **Endangered**, CITES **Appendix I**.
- **Project Tiger: 1973**; **NTCA** statutory authority; **M-STr IPES** supports monitoring/patrolling.
- 2022 All India Tiger Estimation: estimated **3, 682**, range **3, 167-3, 925**. The source uses 3, 167 without explaining that it is the lower bound. [Official estimate](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2076921&lang=1&reg=3).
- Source highlights MP, Karnataka, Uttarakhand; Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam landscape in AP/Telangana; Sundarbans mangrove tigers; Corbett reserve. Rankings require a stated metric/year.
- International cooperation: **Global Tiger Forum**; **TX2** goal sought to double wild tiger numbers by 2022.
## January 2025 recovery study
- **“Tiger recovery amid people and poverty”**: tiger **occupancy expanded ~30%** to **~138, 200 km²**; this is not a 30% population rise. Protected breeding areas and connected multiple-use landscapes support coexistence; source cites ~66 million people in occupied landscapes. [NTCA account](https://ntca.gov.in/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Stripes_Vol14_1_Jul25_compressed.pdf).
| Census year | National estimate |
| --- | --- |
| 2006 | 1, 411 |
| 2010 | 1, 706 |
| 2014 | 2, 226 |
| 2018 | 2, 967 |
| 2022 | **3, 682**, range **3, 167–3, 925** |
- Source labels **2, 226** and **3, 167** as 2024: incorrect. **2, 226 = 2014**; **3, 167 = 2022 lower estimate**, not final central estimate. [Official census comparison](https://www.pib.gov.in/Pressreleaseshare.aspx?PRID=2076921&lang=2&reg=48).
- **Project Tiger 1973**, initially nine reserves; NTCA statutory foundation **2006 amendment**, not 2005. Source 53-reserve count is dated and should not be memorised as current.
- *Panthera tigris*: IUCN **Endangered**, **CITES Appendix I**; commercial international trade tightly restricted, not every exceptional transaction absolutely banned. Wildlife hunting prohibition has statutory exceptions.
- Recall: **Corbett—Uttarakhand; Bandipur—Karnataka/Nilgiri landscape; Kanha—MP; Sundarbans—West Bengal and Bangladesh mangroves; Nagarjunasagar–Srisailam—AP/Telangana landscape**.
- **M-STr IPES** supports patrol/ecological monitoring; conflict prevention, corridors, prey recovery, livelihood support and locally applicable compensation matter. Source “TOES” scheme name and uniform ₹5 lakh compensation are unverified.
- **Global Tiger Initiative 2008**, **TX2** doubling ambition adopted 2010 for 2022; distinguish targets and census methods. WWF **73% decline** refers to average monitored vertebrate-population size **1970–2020**, not 73% of species becoming extinct.

## NTCA institutional recall
- Statutory **2006 wildlife-law amendment**, **Mo EFCC**; Union Environment Minister chair, Minister of State vice-chair, **three MPs**, Ministry Secretary and other specified members.
- Project Tiger oversight, Centre–State accountability/Mo Us, parliamentary oversight and livelihood interests around reserves; NTCA is distinct from NBWL and State field administrations.

## Trail Guard AI in Similipal, February 2025
- Compact cameras perform **edge inference**, classify humans/animals/vehicles and send alerts using **cellular communication**; source reports **30–40 seconds**, low-power operation and **six months–one year** battery life.
- Field-response chain: image classification →control room →patrol communication via VHF/other channels →investigation. Satellite transmission is not the source's described normal link.
- Source reports **96 arrests /86 guns in ten months**, units around **₹50, 000–53, 000**, deployment in **five States /over 14 sites**; dated operational claims. Predicted **80% poaching reduction** is a forecast, not a measured causal result.
- Reduce false positives, protect sensitive location data and distinguish poaching from lawful livelihood activity. Community consultation, access arrangements and forest-rights safeguards build trust.
## Similipal recall
- **Barehipani /Joranda waterfalls**; Budhabalanga, Khairi and Salandi rivers; mixed deciduous/semi-evergreen habitats, elephants and pseudo-melanistic tigers.
- Communities include **Santhal, Kol, Bhumij, Mankidia**; Mankidia are a **PVTG**. Traditional cultural practice does not automatically exempt prohibited wildlife hunting.
- Biosphere designation **2009**; boundaries/status of biosphere, sanctuary, tiger reserve and national park differ. Source's **“National Park 1979”** is not a reliable gazette date; do not memorise it.
- Practice: edge inference true; “continuous high power /satellite transmission” false. **Dudhsagar—Goa /Athirappilly—Kerala** are outside Similipal. Practice questions have no official exam year.

- **Later status clarification: 24 April 2025**, Odisha formally notified **845.70 km² Similipal National Park**; distinguish this from the much larger tiger/biosphere landscape. [Odisha notification announcement](https://inpr.odisha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2025-04/News-Forest_24042025EEEE.pdf).

## Madhav and source corrections
- **Madhav Tiger Reserve, Shivpuri, MP: notified 7 March 2025**, India's 58 th; source 2024 year is wrong. Dry-deciduous forest, grassland/wetlands; reintroduction began 2023. [NTCA minutes](https://ntca.gov.in/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Minutes.pdf).
- MP'snine at this checkpoint:Kanha, Bandhavgarh, Pench, Satpura, Panna, Sanjay-Dubri, Veerangana Durgavati, Ratapani, Madhav.
- **Pantheratigris:IUCNEndangered, notspecies-wide Critically Endangered**; CITESAppendix I restricts international commercial trade, not literally every permitted scientific movement.
- National estimates:2006:1, 411; 2010:1, 706; 2014:2, 226; 2018:2, 967; 2022 minimum 3, 167/estimated 3, 682. Source 2, 226“2024”and 3, 167“2024”misdate different estimates.
- Source“30%growth overtwo decades”should not replace the national numerical trend; growth in occupied area/period-specific study measures differs from total population growth.
- NTCA/WCCB statutory provisions followed **2006 amendment**, not 2005. Section 9 hunting prohibition has statutory exceptions; no universal ₹5 lakhcompensation rule covers every State/case.
- Project Tiger 1973 startednine; source 53 and 58 referdifferentcheckpoints. Listed Dampa twice and omitted Ranipur, UP: corrected State list below. [NTCA](https://ntca.gov.in/faqs/).
## Source-era 58 reserve map list
| State | Reserves |
| --- | --- |
| Andhra Pradesh |Nagarjunsagar–Srisailam|
| Arunachal Pradesh |Namdapha, Pakke, Kamlang|
| Assam |Manas, Nameri, Kaziranga, Orang|
| Bihar |Valmiki|
| Chhattisgarh |Udanti–Sitanadi, Indravati, Achanakmar, Guru Ghasidas–Tamor Pingla|
| Jharkhand |Palamau|
| Karnataka |Nagarahole, Kali, BRT, Bhadra, Bandipur|
| Kerala |Periyar, Parambikulam|
| Madhya Pradesh |Satpura, Sanjay-Dubri, Pench, Panna, Kanha, Bandhavgarh, Veerangana Durgavati, Ratapani, Madhav|
| Maharashtra |Tadoba–Andhari, Melghat, Pench, Sahyadri, Nawegaon–Nagzira, Bor|
| Mizoram |Dampa|
| Odisha |Similipal, Satkosia|
| Rajasthan |Ranthambore, Sariska, Mukundara Hills, Ramgarh Vishdhari, Dholpur–Karauli|
| Tamil Nadu |KMTR, Anamalai, Mudumalai, Sathyamangalam, Srivilliputhur–Megamalai|
| Telangana |Amrabad, Kawal|
| Uttar Pradesh |Dudhwa, Pilibhit, Ranipur|
| Uttarakhand |Corbett, Rajaji|
| West Bengal |Sundarban, Buxa|
## Coexistence and monitoring
- Land sparing protects breeding cores; land sharing/corridors support movement/genetic exchange. Livelihood support, conflict response and community participation accompany habitat protection.
- Poaching, infrastructure, mining, prey depletion and climate pressures differ locally; economic prosperity/conflict associations are not single-cause explanations.
- **M-STr IPES:Monitoring Systemfor Tigers–Intensive Protectionand Ecological Status**; field records/patrol monitoring, not just tracking every tiger with GPS.
- GTI2008/Global Tiger Forum/TX2 doubling goal are different initiatives; India did not alone create/lead every global mechanism.
- WWF's 73%Living Planet Index decline concerns average monitored vertebrate population abundance, not 73%of every species or all individual wild animals disappearing.

## National-park notification: April 2025
- **24 April 2025:** Odisha notified **845.70 km²** as Similipal National Park; the April 29 issue reports it as India's **107th** and Odisha's second/largest, after Bhitarkanika. National-park area differs from the roughly **2,750 km² tiger-reserve landscape**. [Odisha announcement](https://inpr.odisha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2025-04/News-Forest_24042025EEEE.pdf).
- Sanctuary status dates to **1979**, Project Tiger inclusion **1973**, UNESCO biosphere-network inclusion **2009**; overlapping designations have different boundaries and functions. Additional river recall: Palpala, Bandan and Salandi alongside Budhabalanga, Khairi and Deo.
- **Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, section 35:** State notification; boundary alteration requires NBWL recommendation. Grazing is prohibited; habitat destruction/removal and wildlife use face statutory restrictions/exceptions. Do not infer that every type of protected area shares identical legal protection.
- FRA rights recognition and lawful critical-wildlife-habitat procedures matter; national-park notification alone does not automatically extinguish forest rights or authorise displacement.
- Stronger habitat enforcement must accompany corridors, conflict response, trained staff, community consultation and regulated tourism. Climate risks remain; Aichi targets are the earlier framework, not a new 2025 target cycle.

topics.title: IN-SPACe, POEM and SpaDeX
topics.subject: Science and Technology
topics.markdown:
## Institutions and platform
- **IN-SPACe**, under Department of Space: promotes, authorises and facilitates non-government space activities and access to infrastructure.
- **POEM** repurposes PSLV's spent fourth stage (**PS4**) into an orbital experimental platform: cheaper microgravity testing and space qualification without each experiment needing a full satellite.
## Mission facts
- **PSLV-C60/SpaDeX launched 30 December 2024**, not 18 December 2023 as printed in the source. [ISRO mission summary](https://new1.isro.gov.in/Atomospheric_Re_entry_of_POEM4.html).
- **POEM-4 carried 24 payloads: 14 ISRO/DoS + 10 non-government**, including academia/startups through IN-SPACe. SpaDeX satellites and hosted POEM payloads serve distinct experimental purposes. [ISRO payload details](https://www.isro.gov.in/POEM_4_Payloads_spadex.html).
## Mains significance
- Lower entry costs, private innovation, jobs, public-private collaboration, technology validation and downstream communication/navigation/science services.
- Needs: authorisation clarity, affordable infrastructure, safety/debris management, finance and competitive technology. Private participation does not mean privatisation of ISRO.
## POEM-4: plants and walking robotics
- **CROPS — Compact Research Module for Orbital Plant Studies**: cowpea germination under microgravity, reported within **four days**; automated thermal/environment control and a two-leaf-stage objective. A germination experiment does not yet establish a complete sustainable food system. [ISRO CROPS](https://www.isro.gov.in/CROPS.html).
- **RRM-TD — Relocatable Robotic Manipulator–Technology Demonstrator**, developed by **IISU**: **seven degrees of freedom**; relocates itself to defined targets using **inchworm walking**, rather than simply relocating objects. Potential: inspection, assembly and servicing. [ISRO payload description](https://www.isro.gov.in/ISRO_EN/POEM_4_Payloads_spadex.html).

## SpaDeX milestone, 16 January 2025
- **SDX-01 + SDX-02**, roughly **220 kg each**, successfully docked in orbit after earlier postponements. Rendezvous brings craft together; docking physically joins them; combined control/power transfer are further steps. [ISRO docking confirmation](https://www.isro.gov.in/spadex_docking.html).
- Enables orbital assembly/resupply, satellite servicing and future **Chandrayaan-4** sample-return architecture; demonstrates enabling technology, not a fully operational space station or every interplanetary capability.
- Source BAS “end of decade” needs distinction between initial module plans and full station ambition. **POEM/cowpea germination** remains a separate hosted experiment from docking.
- Mains: sustained funding, skilled teams, safe iterative testing, international/private cooperation and clear national-use/research priorities. Source's 250-word/15-mark daily question is coaching practice, not a verified UPSC PYQ.

## Third Launch Pad approval, January 2025
- **Cabinet, 16 January 2025**: **SDSC Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh**, proposed **Third Launch Pad**, **₹3,984.86 crore**, **48 months** target. Approval/schedule are not completion.
- Supports **Next Generation Launch Vehicle**, **LVM3 with semi-cryogenic stages**, enlarged NGLV configurations; standby for **Second Launch Pad**, future human-spaceflight/greater launch frequency.
- Share existing facilities, adaptable design and industry participation; redundancy reduces disruption but construction/qualification must be completed. [Cabinet decision](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2093358&lang=2&reg=48).
- **First Launch Pad** serves **PSLV/SSLV**, source about 30 years old; **Second** serves **GSLV/LVM3** and PSLV backup, about 20 years. Ages are January 2025 approximations.
- The repeated SpaDeX section adds no separate docking event; consolidated milestone remains **16 January 2025**.

## SpaDeX milestones
- PSLV-C60 launched SDX-01 and SDX-02 on 30 December 2024; each approximately 220 kg, targeting a roughly 460 km orbit.
- First docking: **16 January 2025**. Successful undocking: **13 March 2025, about 09:20 IST**. [ISRO](https://www.isro.gov.in/spadex_undocking_successful.html).
- Later milestone: second docking on 20 April and power transfer on **21 April 2025**. Power transfer had not already been demonstrated on 13 March. [ISRO milestone record](https://www.isro.gov.in/Spadex_Successful_demonstration_of_Second_Docking_and_Power_Transfer.html).
- Rendezvous, docking and power-sharing support future stations, sample return and servicing. They do not mean every planned mission or refuelling capability is already operational.

## 12 August 2025: commercial Earth-observation PPP selection
- **IN-SPACe selected a PixxelSpace India-led consortium** with **PierSight Space, SatSure Analytics India and Dhruva Space** to design, build and operate a commercial EO constellation. Source plan: **12 satellites, investment over₹1,200 crore across five years**; selection/commitment is not launch or full deployment. [IN-SPACe announcement](https://www.inspace.gov.in/).
- Planned data/services support agriculture, flood/fire/disaster management, climate, urban infrastructure, marine surveillance and national security. Indigenous capability improves data sovereignty; it cannot promise complete elimination of specialised/global foreign data.
- **Analysis Ready Data (ARD)** is preprocessed for analysis; **Value-Added Services (VAS)** transform observations into products such as crop-health indices/flood-risk maps. Optical/infrared/radar sensors have different weather/light capabilities.
- **Oceansat-2**, launched **23 September 2009**: **OCM-2** ocean colour/chlorophyll/sediment; **Ku-band scatterometer** ocean-surface winds; Italian **ROSA** radio occultation for atmospheric profiles. These explain **2010 PYQ: all three(d)**—water-vapour estimation, monsoon-onset prediction and coastal-pollution monitoring. [ISRO mission](https://new1.isro.gov.in/Oceansat_2.html).
- EO practice intended **1,2,3 only**, which is **option2**, despite printed answer saying “option3”; fourth statement claiming complete replacement of foreign data is false.

topics.title: Former prime ministers: state funerals and memorials
topics.subject: Governance in India
topics.markdown:
## December 2024 context
- Manmohan Singh died **26 December 2024**; seven-day mourning and a state funeral; cremated at **Nigambodh Ghat on 28 December**.
- Source account distinguishes state-funeral guidelines from **the absence of a specific rule mandating a memorial for every former PM**. Past commemorative practice is not itself a constitutional entitlement.
- MHA subsequently conveyed a commitment to allocate memorial space; retain this as the source's December 2024 account, not a claim about today's allocation status.
## Memorial associations
- Nehru - **Shanti Van**; Shastri - **Vijay Ghat**; Charan Singh - **Kisan Ghat**; Indira Gandhi - **Shakti Sthal**; Rajiv Gandhi - **Vir Bhumi**; P.V. Narasimha Rao - **Ekta Sthal**; Vajpayee - **Sadaiv Atal** at Smriti Sthal.
- Source notes exceptions/local sites, including V.P. Singh and Morarji Desai's Ahmedabad samadhi. Avoid its inconsistent assertion that every memorial is in/near Delhi.
- Upkeep depends on the site and responsible government/trust; source reports Vajpayee's memorial funded by Atal Smriti Nyas, Rs 10.51 crore.
## Governance link
- Clear, consistent criteria, transparent allocation and preservation of public commemorative spaces.

topics.title: Core industries and industrial indicators
topics.subject: Indian Economy
topics.markdown:
## Eight core industries
- **Coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilisers, steel, cement, electricity.**
- Index of Eight Core Industries (**ICI**) is a weighted output index; monthly release by **Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT**. The source series uses **2011-12** as base year.
## Source-series weights (%)
| Industry | Weight |
| --- | ---: |
| Refinery products | 28.04 |
| Electricity | 19.85 |
| Steel | 17.92 |
| Coal | 10.33 |
| Crude oil | 8.98 |
| Natural gas | 6.88 |
| Cement | 5.37 |
| Fertilisers | 2.63 |
## How to use
- Measure sector output relative to the base period; weights represent the constituent sectors within the index, not each sector's share of the entire economy.
- Infrastructure and manufacturing are linked through steel/cement, fuel and power; changes have downstream effects on construction, transport and finance.
- Published near month-end for the previous month's output, before that month's IIP release; distinguish growth rate from index level.
## Read the index
- Monthly business survey comparing conditions with the **previous month**; a timely indicator of manufacturing/services activity, not a direct measurement of GDP growth.
| Reading | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Above 50 | Expansion compared with previous month |
| 50 | No change |
| Below 50 | Contraction |
- **58 → 54:** slower expansion, not contraction. **46 → 49:** slower contraction, not expansion. Distinguish level from direction of change.
- A diffusion index uses respondents reporting improvement plus half those reporting no change, with relevant weighting/seasonal adjustment.
## Components and comparison
- S&P Global manufacturing headline: **new orders 30%, output 25%, employment 20%, suppliers’ delivery times 15% (inverted), stocks of purchases 10%**. [S&P methodology](https://www.spglobal.com/market-intelligence/en/news-insights/research/sp-global-pmi-and-ism-survey-comparisons).
- Services business-activity and composite-output measures differ from simply averaging every manufacturing headline component.
- Longer delivery times can reflect demand pressure **or supply disruption**; a headline alone can mislead. [S&P interpretation](https://www.spglobal.com/market-intelligence/en/news-insights/research/understanding-headline-pmi-vs-subindices-how-signals-can-be-lost-by-focusing-exclusively-on-the-headline-pmi).
- **PMI:** survey signals on orders/output/jobs and other conditions, usually released early. **IIP:** official measured industrial production, covering mining, manufacturing and electricity with a later publication lag.
- Useful to policymakers, firms and investors alongside inflation, credit, jobs and official output data; it does not mechanically determine RBI rates or guarantee stock-market gains. Indian PMI is compiled by **S&P Global**; IHS Markit is the predecessor name, not a separate current compiler.

## Index of Industrial Production
- **IIP:** measured industrial output in **mining, manufacturing and electricity**; monthly **NSO, MoSPI** release. Source-series base **2011–12**; formerly associated with CSO, now part of NSO.
- Weighted volume index using a fixed-base/Laspeyres approach; compare the same relevant period for growth.
- **Index 116 =16% above base output**, not automatically 16% year-on-year growth. Positive index value ≠positive growth; falling positive values can indicate contraction.
- Eight core industries contribute about **40.27%** of that IIP series, not 40.27% of all GDP. IIP excludes most services and differs from value-added GDP and survey-based PMI.

## IIP revision
- IIP measures weighted changes in industrial production volumes: mining, manufacturing and electricity; excludes agriculture and most services. NSO publishes it.
- The base in the March 2025 source period was 2011–12. Index 116 means 16% above the base level, **not 16% year-on-year growth**.
- A positive index value does not prove production rose that month; compare the appropriate periods. IIP is an output indicator, not a direct inflation measure.

## April 2025 IIP release
- **28 May 2025 quick estimate:** industrial production grew **2.7% year on year in April**, against the **3.0% March quick estimate**. It is a slowing growth rate, not a 2.7% fall in output. [MoSPI release](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2025/may/doc2025528559501.pdf).
- The issue's remaining IIP definition, sector coverage, volume-index method and **2011–12 base** repeat existing notes. Compiler is **NSO, MoSPI**, not an independent current CSO; index **116** means 16% above the base, not automatically 16% annual growth. IIP is not a price index or a full GDP measure.

## May 2025 manufacturing survey
- Contemporary June 2 release reports **HSBC India Manufacturing PMI 57.6 in May, versus 58.2 in April**: softer expansion, not contraction. Contents refers to the May low, but the reproduced generic body does not print the figure. **57.6 is an index reading, not 57.6% output growth**. [Contemporary release record](https://www.cmegroup.com/education/events/econoday/636975).
- HSBC is the India-series sponsor in this period; S&P Global compiles the survey. Existing definitions, components and IIP comparison cover the repeated text.

topics.title: Green steel and industrial decarbonisation
topics.subject: Indian Economy
topics.markdown:
## Policy status in December 2024
- Ministry of Steel was **preparing** a Green Steel Mission with estimated cost **Rs 15,000 crore**. The January PDF overstates this as an already implemented investment.
- Proposed elements: green-steel PLI, renewable-energy incentives and public procurement. Green-steel taxonomy released **12 December 2024**; decarbonisation roadmap drew on **14 task forces**. [Ministry review](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2088827&lang=2&reg=48).
## Transition levers
- Renewable electricity + energy efficiency; scrap recycling; hydrogen-based **direct reduced iron (DRI)**; carbon capture where technically/economically suitable.
- Related policies: National Steel Policy 2017 (300 Mt capacity ambition for 2030-31), Steel Scrap Recycling Policy 2019, Vehicle Scrapping Policy 2021 and National Green Hydrogen Mission.
## Dated industry context and trade-offs
- Source reports **139.15 Mt finished-steel production in 2023-24**; distinguish finished-steel output from crude-steel production/capacity.
- Gains: lower emissions/pollution, export competitiveness and green skills. Barriers: costly capital/hydrogen, reliable clean power, technology scale-up and financing for smaller producers.
- Way forward: R&D, pilots, standards, demand creation, PPPs and international technology/finance cooperation; align expansion with net-zero **2070**.
## Production routes and measurable decarbonisation
| Route / intervention | Carbon implication |
| --- | --- |
| Blast furnace → basic oxygen furnace | Coke supplies heat and reduces ore; replacing its functions is difficult |
| DRI → electric arc furnace | Hydrogen can replace carbon-based reducing agents; benefits depend on hydrogen and electricity production |
| Scrap → electric furnace | Avoids much primary ore reduction; scrap quality, availability and clean power matter |
| CCUS | Potential residual-emission reduction; needs economical capture, transport and verified storage |
- **Coal gasification does not inherently produce low-carbon steel**; electricity or hydrogen is low-carbon only with a suitable production pathway. Reduce emissions per tonne and total emissions as output grows.
- India's **12 December 2024 taxonomy** defines green steel below **2.2 tCO2e per tonne of finished steel**: five stars below 1.6; four stars 1.6–2.0; three stars 2.0–2.2. Certification uses measured intensity; “green” does not mean guaranteed zero emissions. [Steel Ministry brochure](https://steel.gov.in/sites/default/files/2025-03/Taxonomy%20Brochure.pdf).
## Industrial policy and constraints
- Steel underpins infrastructure, vehicles, engineering and defence. Specialty-steel PLI has an approved **₹6,322-crore** outlay ([Cabinet approval](https://www.pib.gov.in/Pressreleaseshare.aspx?PRID=1737723&lang=2&reg=48)); quality-control orders require specified BIS conformity for covered products. Logistics planning through PM Gati Shakti connects production centres to transport, ports and energy infrastructure.
- Carbon prices, green public procurement and credible product standards can create demand; renewable power, affordable hydrogen and pilots can reduce production costs. Hydrogen storage/transport, furnace conversion, finance for smaller plants and geological storage assessment constrain scaling.
- Source's 300-Mt National Steel Policy goal means **crude-steel capacity by 2030–31**, not guaranteed actual production in 2030. Its 2050 output, cost and export-loss figures are model-dependent projections.
## PYQ revision
- **2015, coking coal (c):** India imports suitable metallurgical coal for coke-based steelmaking; saltpetre and rock phosphate are not the answer.
- **2014, pollutants (d):** steelmaking can emit all four listed gases—sulphur oxides, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide. Air-pollution controls, wastewater treatment and waste management complement carbon reduction.

## April 23 additions: steel governance and scenario reading
- **National Metallurgist Award**, Ministry of Steel: recognises metallurgical contributions. Source describes **25 minimum safety guidelines**, informed by ILO iron/steel safety practice and World Steel Association principles; occupational safety accompanies emission reduction.
- Source's **FY2022–23** output snapshots (**125.32 Mt crude; 121.29 Mt finished**) and **FY2021–22 ~2% GDP** are dated figures, not April 2025 production totals. Major producing belts include Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Gujarat and West Bengal; rankings need a stated production measure/year.
- National Solar Mission began **January 2010**; renewable electricity can lower steelmaking emissions. **Kalyani FeRRESTA** is a company green-steel brand, not a government steelmaking programme or proof that all production is fossil-free.
- Model claims in the source—**435 Mt output in 2050**, **$500 billion cumulative coking-coal forex savings**, **58% EU export loss without decarbonisation**, hydrogen break-even at **$1/kg**, or competitiveness at **$2/kg with a $50/tCO2 carbon price**—are conditional projections, not policy targets or guaranteed outcomes.
- Likewise quoted green/grey hydrogen prices and **₹3.2 lakh per tonne** plant-cost figures are dated assumptions (the latter lacks a clear capacity denominator); compare full system costs, financing, ore quality, electricity and carbon-price conditions.
- Its steel-emissions figures mix **2018 direct sector emissions (~270 MtCO2e)** with other years/boundaries; do not add its 9%, 10% and 11% shares. Purchased-electricity emissions, national greenhouse gases and energy-related CO2 have different denominators.

## May 14 additions: product categories and data correction
- **Flat steel:** plates/sheets; **long steel:** bars/rods/sections; specialty grades meet particular performance needs. Tata Steel, **SAIL** and JSW illustrate major producers; company capacity rankings require current geographic/consolidation scope.
- Correct the source's **2023 “120 Mt crude steel”**: World Steel Association gives **140.8 Mt in calendar 2023**. FY, calendar-year, finished/crude output and installed capacity differ; the source's company capacities and >150-Mt national capacity are dated snapshots. [World Steel in Figures 2024](https://worldsteel.org/data/world-steel-in-figures/world-steel-in-figures-2024/).
- India imports substantial suitable **coking coal** but has large domestic iron-ore production; avoid equating iron-ore and metallurgical-coal import dependence. Global competition, energy costs and decarbonisation affect export competitiveness.
- Housing/infrastructure and manufacturing can expand demand, but future plant expansions and policy targets are not realised output. Generic references to Steel Development Fund/export incentives need scheme/date verification, not assumed universal subsidies.

topics.title: Landslides and disaster relief
topics.subject: India & World Geography
topics.markdown:
## Wayanad context
- January 2025 source discusses the 2024 Wayanad landslide and the Centre's assessment as a disaster of **severe nature**. It reports 254 deaths and 128 missing; these are reporting-time figures, not final totals.
- Impacts: displacement/trauma, infrastructure and crop losses, livelihood disruption, erosion and ecosystem damage; vulnerable groups need targeted assistance.
## Relief framework
- **Disaster Management Act, 2005**; NDMA for national disaster-policy coordination; SDRF provides state-level immediate relief.
- NDRF may supplement SDRF after assessment and prescribed procedure for severe disasters. **NCCF is the predecessor of NDRF**, not a separate contemporary additional fund as the source suggests. [Official fund explanation](https://ies.gov.in/arthapedia/concept/national-disaster-response-fund-ndrf).
- **NDRF fund ≠ National Disaster Response Force**; use full names to avoid confusion. Relief assistance is not full compensation for every loss.
## Risk reduction
- Hazard mapping, slope-sensitive land use and drainage, resilient roads/buildings, local rainfall monitoring and evacuation protocols; livelihood recovery and psychosocial support.
- Link to **Sendai Framework** and climate adaptation. A tsunami-warning system is a different hazard-specific example, not a landslide detector.
## Himalayan landslide dams
- Alaknanda study discussed on 9 January 2025: landslide blockage → temporary lake → possible dam breach → downstream flood. Risk combines slope failure with flood exposure; monitoring must follow both hazards.

topics.title: Sea otters and trophic cascades
topics.subject: Environment
topics.markdown:
## Identification and ecological role
- **Enhydra lutris**, coastal North Pacific marine mammal, renowned for dense fur and tool use to open shellfish.
- **Keystone predator**: controls sea urchins and helps protect kelp; diet also includes crabs and other invertebrates. Source reports food intake up to 25% of body mass daily.
- California's **Elkhorn Slough** example: otter predation may help control invasive **European green crabs**, which damage native coastal habitats.
## Conservation
- Source lists IUCN **Endangered**; threats include oil spills, pollution, disease, prey/habitat change and climate impacts. Protect habitats, reduce pollution and monitor populations.
- Avoid the source's absolute 'smallest marine mammal' superlative; distinguish sea otters from freshwater/river otters.
## Recall chain
Sea otter predation → fewer grazing sea urchins → healthier kelp habitat → more biodiversity.
