## Article 5 and functions
- **Armed attack on one → treated as attack on all → each ally assists with action it deems necessary, including possible armed force.** It does not prescribe an identical automatic declaration of war by every member.
- Article 5 invoked only once, following **9/11 attacks in 2001**; the initial decision on **12 September** was conditional on the attack being directed from abroad. [NATO Article 5 explanation](https://nato.int/en/what-we-do/introduction-to-nato/collective-defence-and-article-5).
- Political consultation, democratic values, defence planning, deterrence and collective security; diplomacy and peaceful settlement alongside military crisis management.
- Collective-defence operations and other crisis-management missions have different mandates: do not assume every NATO operation invoked Article 5 or that membership follows automatically from cooperation.
- Map recall: **North America + Europe; enlarged Nordic/Baltic security space.** NATO is a security alliance, distinct from the EU.

topics.title: Food safety: contamination, toxins and cold chains
topics.subject: Governance in India
topics.markdown:
## Spoiled coconut water: infection versus poisoning
- The report recycled in April 2025 is not evidence that ordinary fresh coconut water causes brain infection. A **2021 published Danish case** linked fatal encephalopathy to **3-nitropropionic acid**, produced in a spoiled coconut by the fungus *Arthrinium saccharicola*. Investigators considered bongkrekic acid but did not detect it.
- **Encephalopathy = disturbed brain function**; toxic/metabolic encephalopathy does not itself mean microbes infected the brain. Foodborne illness may involve infection, preformed toxins, or both.
- Improper storage permits spoilage and microbial growth. Refrigeration slows growth; it neither sterilises food nor reliably removes toxins already formed. Follow product storage/use-by instructions and reject spoiled products rather than taste-testing them.

**Unsafe storage → microbial growth/toxin formation → ingestion → gastrointestinal illness or systemic harm.**

## Governance and prevention
- **FSSAI:** statutory food regulator under the **Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006**. Prevention requires hygienic handling, safe water, appropriate packaging, traceability, storage labels, and risk-based inspections across the supply chain.
- Protect vulnerable consumers through vendor training and public awareness. Temperature sensors and cold-chain monitoring can flag failures; they supplement testing and enforcement.
- Shared responsibility: producers and sellers ensure safe processing and clear instructions; regulators monitor compliance; consumers follow storage advice. Accountability should rest on evidence, not an assumption that every incident proves seller negligence.

[Primary clinical investigation, CDC Emerging Infectious Diseases](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/27/1/20-2222_article)
## Risk-based regulation: June 2025 editorial
- **Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954 →Food Safety and Standards Act 2006**: consolidated, science-based food regulation. **FSSAI established 2008**, under Health Ministry; the PDF conflates Act year with institutional establishment. Older regulation did contain standards/limits—do not infer it ignored all contaminant distinctions.
- **Hazard:** potential to harm; **risk:** harm likelihood/severity at actual exposure. **MRL**, mg/kg food, is an enforcement limit for a pesticide–commodity pair; **ADI**, usually mg/kg body weight/day, is estimated long-term daily exposure without appreciable health risk. MRL is not itself a toxic-dose threshold, and exceedance does not automatically quantify illness.
- **Total Diet Study (TDS)** assesses population dietary exposure from representative foods, often prepared as consumed. Indian consumption, residues and vulnerable groups matter; imported toxicology data can remain informative while local exposure data improve relevance.
- Editorial identifies gaps in representative national TDS, local data, trained assessors and communication; do not declare every existing Indian exposure estimate invalid or prove all standards attained Codex equivalence by 2020.
- Source **0.01→0.1 mg/kg** example needs pesticide/food/regulatory context; some default-limit discussions concerned **spices/herbs**, not a tenfold relaxation of every pesticide standard. Changes require evidence and transparent exposure assessment; a higher MRL alone neither proves increased toxicity nor automatically proves unchanged safety.

## MSG and communicating evidence
- **Monosodium glutamate** is a flavour additive; glutamate occurs naturally in foods and breast milk. **JECFA 1987 “ADI not specified”** means evaluated uses did not require a numeric ADI, not approval of unlimited doses or every infant-food use. [JECFA evaluation](https://apps.who.int/food-additives-contaminants-jecfa-database/Home/Chemical/2267).
- The editorial critiques infant-warning labels and proposes review; natural occurrence alone does not establish every formulation/dose safe, and a recommendation is not proof labelling rules were repealed.
- Proposals: representative local dietary/contaminant studies, periodic evidence review, staff training, clear charts/units, transparent assumptions, accessible public consultation and accurate uncertainty communication.

## Codex: institution and trade
- **Codex Alimentarius** is the collection of food standards; **Codex Alimentarius Commission (CAC)** is the **FAO/WHO intergovernmental body, founded 1963**, Secretariat/Rome association.
- **189 members =188 countries +EU member organisation**, not 189 countries. Regular FAO/WHO budgets support its work; observer status and membership differ. [Codex membership](https://codex.fao.org/about-codex/who-we-are/members).
- Standards/guidelines/codes are generally **voluntary international texts**, with national enforceability through domestic adoption. **WTO SPS Agreement** recognises Codex food-safety standards as benchmarks; this is not a Codex court deciding every food trade dispute or automatic domestic legal force.
- Scientific expert assessments (**JECFA/JMPR**) underpin ADIs/residue work; distinguish expert risk assessment from CAC adoption/risk management.
- Committees: **CCSCH—Spices/Culinary Herbs, hosted by India; CCCF—Contaminants; CCPR—Pesticide Residues; CCFA—Food Additives**. Hygiene, labelling and contaminant/residue guidance protect health and support fair trade; country-specific stronger measures need applicable scientific/legal justification.

topics.title: Coconut economy and circular value chains
topics.subject: Indian Economy
topics.markdown:
## Crop, institutions and observance
- Coconut is a tropical plantation crop supporting coastal livelihoods; **Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu** are major producing states. The compilation's **20,535.88 million nuts** is a **2022–23 production figure**, not a current annual estimate.
- **Coconut Development Board:** statutory body established **12 January 1981**, headquartered at **Kochi**, under the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare; promotes cultivation, productivity, processing and value addition.
- **International Coconut Community:** intergovernmental organisation formed under UNESCAP's auspices in **1969**; India is a founding member. It is not itself a UN agency.
- **World Coconut Day: 2 September**, observed since **2009**. The **2024 theme** emphasised circular use and partnerships to maximise value.

## Whole-coconut value chain
| Material | Useful products |
|---|---|
| Water and flesh | Beverages, food, milk and processed products |
| Kernel | Oil and value-added foods/cosmetics |
| Husk | Coir fibre and coir-pith products |
| Shell | Handicrafts, charcoal and activated-carbon products |

- Circular processing creates employment and export opportunities while reducing discarded material. Replanting, resilient varieties, irrigation matched to local conditions, pest control, credit, producer aggregation, quality certification and processing research strengthen the sector.
- Risks: drought, erratic rainfall, rising temperatures, ageing palms and post-harvest losses. Water needs and carbon benefits depend on cultivation and processing conditions; coconut is not universally a low-water crop.
- **Health correction:** coconut water can provide fluids and electrolytes; coconut products are not proven cures for diabetes or heart disease. Coconut oil is rich in saturated fat; WHO prefers unsaturated fats to saturated fats.

[World Coconut Day, PIB](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2050123&lang=2&reg=48) · [CDB institutional history](https://coconutboard.gov.in/docs/icj/inj-2021-02.pdf) · [WHO healthy-diet guidance](https://www.who.int/en/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/healthy-diet)

## July 2025 oil-price pressure
- Source reports retail coconut oil near**₹460/kg**; a local/date-specific price, not a fixed national quotation. **Copra**, dried kernel, yields oil used in cooking, soaps, cosmetics and hair products. Source estimates **5.7 lakh tonnes/year**, **3.9 lakh tonnes edible**, without a clear reference year.
- Supply pressures: El Niño/drought in Philippines/Indonesia, ageing palms, long harvest cycles, possible raw-coconut export restrictions and diversion to **coconut methyl ester(CME) biodiesel**. Biofuel and food demand compete for feedstock.
- Source's “third-largest(2023)” and“31.45% of global output(FY 22)” mix periods/measurement; retain year/unit distinctions rather than derive a current rank from them. India/Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala are major production centres; acreage, productivity and total output are different measures.
- The Lakshadweep productivity/oil-content question is **CDS 2024**, excluded from CSE PYQ banks; the unsupported“highest productivity in India” superlative needs year-specific CDB comparison.

topics.title: Agasthyamala Biosphere Reserve
topics.subject: Environment
topics.markdown:
## Location and recognition
- Established **2001** in the southern Western Ghats, spanning **Kerala and Tamil Nadu**; approximately **3,500 km²**.
- Joined UNESCO's **World Network of Biosphere Reserves in 2016**, under the Man and the Biosphere programme. This differs from the **2012 Western Ghats World Heritage inscription**; biosphere-reserve recognition does not mean the entire reserve is one World Heritage property.
- Includes **Shendurney, Peppara and Neyyar wildlife sanctuaries**, and **Kalakkad Mundanthurai Tiger Reserve**. Peaks reach about **1,868 m**.

## Biodiversity and people
- Tropical wet evergreen/montane forests and high-altitude grasslands support elephants, tigers, lion-tailed macaques and diverse amphibians, reptiles and birds.
- UNESCO records **2,254 higher-plant species**, including about **405 endemics**; the reserve also conserves crop genetic resources such as cardamom, pepper, jamun, nutmeg and plantain.
- **Chenkurinji (*Gluta travancorica*)**, family Anacardiaceae, is native to southwest India. Do not equate its native range with only this reserve or treat traditional medicinal uses as established clinical treatments.
- **Kani/Kanikaran communities** contribute ecological and ethnobotanical knowledge. Conservation should respect community rights, participation and equitable benefit sharing; avoid unsupported claims that they are the oldest surviving tribe.

| Zone | Main role |
|---|---|
| Core | Biodiversity conservation and compatible research |
| Buffer | Activities compatible with conservation, education and monitoring |
| Transition | Settlements and sustainable livelihood/development cooperation |

**Protect ecosystems + involve local communities + sustain livelihoods** is the biosphere-reserve model; its zones do not replace applicable national protected-area laws.

[UNESCO reserve profile](https://www.unesco.org/en/mab/agasthyamala) · [Kew species distribution](https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/69644-1)

topics.title: HANSA trainer aircraft and technology transfer
topics.subject: Science and Technology
topics.markdown:
## 4 April 2025 development
- **CSIR–National Aerospace Laboratories (NAL)** licensed **HANSA-3(NG)** know-how to **Pioneer Clean Amps Pvt. Ltd.** for manufacture and commercialisation, including production support and after-sales services.
- Public R&D → licensed private manufacturing → pilot-training capacity: the agreement supports domestic aerospace supply chains, skilled employment and potential exports. A technology licence is distinct from aircraft certification or delivery.

## Aircraft recall
- **Two-seat, all-composite light trainer**, designed and developed by CSIR-NAL for basic flying training. Composite construction offers low weight; the bubble canopy improves visibility, while dual controls support instruction.
- NG features include a **Rotax digitally controlled engine**, glass cockpit and electrically operated flaps. Indigenous design does not imply every component is Indian: Rotax is a foreign engine supplier.
- The original HANSA programme predates 1998; **HANSA-3 received DGCA certification in February 2000**. Do not label the 2025 licence India's first-ever indigenous aircraft manufacture.
- Domestic trainer availability can reduce dependence on imported training aircraft; sustained benefits require regulatory certification, production quality, maintenance networks and viable operating costs.

[Technology-transfer announcement, PIB](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleaseIframePage.aspx?PRID=2118821&lang=2&reg=48) · [CSIR original HANSA history](https://www.csir.res.in/en/csir-success-stories/hansa-two-seat-aircraft-pilot-training) · [NAL HANSA programme](https://hansang.nal.res.in/)

topics.title: Ottawa Convention and humanitarian disarmament
topics.subject: International Relations
topics.markdown:
## Treaty essentials
- **Ottawa Convention / Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention:** adopted at Oslo in September **1997**, opened for signature at Ottawa; effective **1 March 1999**. India, Russia, China and the US are not parties.
- Bans **anti-personnel** mines: use, development, production, acquisition, stockpiling and transfer, including assistance with prohibited activities. It does **not** ban every anti-vehicle mine or cover cluster munitions under the same treaty.
- **Four years:** destroy stocks, apart from the minimum retained for permitted detection/clearance/destruction training. **Ten years:** clear mined areas under jurisdiction/control; authorised extensions are possible. Both deadlines run from entry into force **for that State**, not signature.
- Article 6 covers international cooperation and victim assistance. **Article 20:** withdrawal requires notice/reasons; normally effective six months after depositary receipt. If the State is then engaged in armed conflict, effectiveness waits until the conflict ends. Other international-law duties continue. [UN treaty text](https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1997/09/19970918%2007-53%20AM/Ch_XXVI_05p.pdf).
## March–April 2025: security versus civilian protection
- Poland and the Baltic states—**Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania**—announced plans in March; Finland followed in early April. These were **announcements, not completed withdrawals** at the 6 April news date. Governments cited Russia-related threats and defensive flexibility. [Lithuanian Defence Ministry](https://kam.lt/en/lithuania-withdraws-from-the-anti-personnel-mine-ban-convention/).
- Mines persist after fighting: casualties, inaccessible farmland, delayed return/reconstruction and costly clearance. The ICRC's **4 April 2025** statement reported over 80% of victims were civilians. Norway remained committed in the source-period discussion. [ICRC statement](https://www.icrc.org/en/news-release/wars-raging-tensions-rising-we-must-uphold-vision-of-landmine-free-world).
- **Separate treaty:** Convention on Cluster Munitions, **2008**. Lithuania's withdrawal already became effective **6 March 2025**; it was not merely under consideration. Unexploded submunitions create a long-term civilian hazard. [ICRC](https://www.icrc.org/en/article/reneging-cluster-munitions-ban-endangers-civilian-lives-and-erodes-ihl).
## Mains revision
- Weigh asserted deterrence benefits against indiscriminate harm, treaty credibility, post-conflict livelihoods and victim-care costs. Withdrawal does not remove humanitarian-law obligations.
- Priorities: sustained clearance funding, rehabilitation/social inclusion, risk education, security dialogue and compliant defensive alternatives. **Self-deactivation does not make an otherwise prohibited anti-personnel mine lawful under this Convention.** Foreign-aid interruptions can slow clearance; the source's claim that a 2025 review restarted programmes in 2024 is chronologically inconsistent.

topics.title: RAPID-CRISPR and leukaemia diagnosis
topics.subject: Science and Technology
topics.markdown:
## Disease and Indian innovation
- **APL = acute promyelocytic leukaemia**, an aggressive blood cancer usually associated with **PML::RARA fusion**. Dangerous bleeding makes rapid recognition/treatment critical; it is highly treatable with timely specialist care.
- **ACTREC, Tata Memorial Centre**, under the Department of Atomic Energy, developed RAPID-CRISPR; the study appeared in **Blood Advances, February 2025**. CRISPR means **Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats** and derives from microbial defence systems.
## Diagnostic pathway
**Sample preparation → RT-LAMP amplification → Cas12a target recognition → reporter cleavage → visible lateral-flow signal.**
- LAMP is **loop-mediated isothermal amplification**; RNA is reverse-transcribed and amplified without PCR-style temperature cycling. Cas12a recognition of the fusion-associated target triggers a reporter signal.
- The study tested conventional extracted-RNA workflows and a simplified **extraction-free preparation coupled with RT-LAMP**. The source's assertion of **no genetic amplification** is incorrect: amplification remains part of the assay.
- Reported **100% sensitivity and specificity apply to the study samples**, not every future patient/field setting. Blood or bone-marrow specimens can be used; speed and simpler readout support resource-limited diagnosis.
- This is **diagnostic detection, not gene-editing treatment**. Wider use needs external validation, quality control, training and prompt referral/treatment access. [Primary study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11808594/).
## Public-health relevance
- Affordable near-patient testing can reduce diagnostic delays and geographical inequity. Procurement, laboratory networks and referral pathways matter alongside the invention.
- Programme integration suggested by the coaching article is a **policy proposal**, not proof the test was already nationally rolled out or included in Ayushman Bharat.

topics.title: Kancha Gachibowli: urban commons and land monetisation
topics.subject: Environment
topics.markdown:
## April 2025 dispute
- **Kancha Gachibowli, Hyderabad, Telangana:** proposed monetisation of approximately **400 acres** of green land within/adjacent to the University of Hyderabad campus triggered student protests and litigation. State revenue needs, academic land claims and ecological protection intersect.
- UoH was founded in **1974**, following the **Six-Point Formula of 1973**; the formula itself is not dated 1974. [University background](https://uohyd.ac.in/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/International-Conference_Brochure.pdf).
- The source traces earlier allocation of about 2,324 acres, later diversions to public institutions, and a **2004 IMG sports-project deal involving 534 acres**, followed by cancellation and litigation. Allocation, possession, registered title and environmental permission are separate legal issues; the State's ownership claim does not resolve every ecological or university claim.
## Why an urban green commons matters
- Vegetation, rocks and water bodies provide habitat continuity, groundwater recharge, flood buffering, heat moderation and research/recreation space. Land can have substantial ecological value even without being a formally notified sanctuary.
- The source reports **233 bird species and 72 tree species from campus-level biodiversity work**; these counts cannot automatically be assigned to the disputed 400 acres. Its claim of 27 Schedule-I birds requires matching the survey and applicable amended schedules.
- **Murricia hyderabadensis**, a spider, is a recognised species. The claim that it occurs only at Kancha Gachibowli is unsupported: published records exist elsewhere. [World Spider Catalog](https://www.wsc.nmbe.ch/spec-data/19675); [research record](https://www.biodiversityjournal.com/images/pubblicazioni/biodiversity-journal-2025/biodiversity-journal-2025-16-03/biodiversity-journal-2025-16-03_541-551.pdf).
## Court intervention and legal principles
- **3 April 2025:** Supreme Court initiated suo motu proceedings, ordered an urgent site inspection/report and directed that **no tree felling be permitted until further orders**. It expressly allowed parallel High Court proceedings to continue. This interim order was not a final determination of ownership or auction legality. [Supreme Court order](https://api.sci.gov.in/supremecourt/2025/17597/17597_2025_2_810_60673_Order_03-Apr-2025.pdf).
- **Article 21**, environmental duties under **Articles 48A and 51A(g)**, public trust, precaution and intergenerational equity provide the analytical framework; their application depends on facts and applicable law.
## Mains framework
- Fiscal stress → land-sale incentive → irreversible habitat loss → public litigation → accountable alternatives.
- Require transparent land records, independent ecological assessment, community/university consultation and lawful clearances. Evaluate alternative revenue sources and brownfield development before sacrificing connected green space.
- Ethics: stewardship of public assets, present welfare versus future generations, procedural fairness and the difference between market price and ecological/social value. Auction receipts are one-time income; recurring fiscal needs require durable financing.

topics.title: Healthy diets: affordability and hidden hunger
topics.subject: Social Problems In India
topics.markdown:
## Calories are not complete nutrition
- A staple-heavy diet may meet energy needs while lacking protein quality, vitamins and minerals. A healthy diet requires **diversity, adequacy, balance and moderation**; cheap calories alone do not ensure nutritional security.
- **SOFI 2024, using 2022 data:** **2.826 billion people / 35.4%** could not afford a healthy diet; average cost **3.96 PPP dollars per person per day**. These are dated estimates, not a current headcount or US retail-dollar price. The source's “three billion” and $3.67 figures should not be mixed with this dataset. [FAO](https://fao.sitefinity.cloud/newsroom/detail/healthy-diets-remain-unaffordable-for-a-third-of-the-world-s-population/en).
- Affordability depends on income after essential non-food needs and local food prices; the statement that everyone in India must spend all income on food is false. Subsistence farming also need not supply a nutritionally diverse diet.
## Hidden hunger and unequal access
- **Hidden hunger:** micronutrient deficiency, e.g. iron, iodine or vitamin A, even where calories or body weight appear adequate.
- Effects include anaemia, impaired growth/cognition, weaker immunity and lower productivity; maternal and child deprivation can perpetuate disadvantage across generations. Undernutrition and obesity can coexist.
- Poverty, gender inequality, price shocks, weak cold chains, limited local markets and incentives favouring staple monocultures restrict access to diverse foods.
## Policy: nutrition security
- Diversify **PDS, Anganwadi/ICDS services under POSHAN and school meals / PM POSHAN** with locally appropriate nutrient-rich foods; fortification supplements dietary diversity rather than replacing it.
- Promote pulses, millets, fruits/vegetables, kitchen gardens and nutrition-sensitive agriculture; **2023 was the International Year of Millets**. Align incentives with nutritional and ecological outcomes.
- Improve storage/cold chains, reduce perishables loss, support farmer-market links, protect household purchasing power and strengthen nutrition education.
- **SDG 2** (Zero Hunger), **SDG 3** (health), **UDHR Article 25** (adequate standard of living including food); EAT-Lancet connects dietary health with environmental sustainability, not a binding food entitlement.
- Revision chain: low income + high nutritious-food prices → poor dietary diversity → hidden hunger → poorer learning/productivity → persistent poverty. Break the cycle through income support, diverse supply and accessible nutrition services.

## SOFI 2025 and nutrition-sensitive food systems
- Issue reports **673 million / 8.2% globally undernourished in 2024**, down from **688 million in 2023**, while regional inequalities persist. India's prevalence reportedly declined **14.3% in 2020–22 → 12% in 2022–24**, about **30 million fewer people**. Global annual estimates and India's three-year averages are different reference periods; revisions across report editions also matter. [FAO's SOFI 2025 presentation](https://india.un.org/en/301406-fao-presents-sofi-2025-report-new-delhi).
- Digital PDS mechanisms—Aadhaar-linked records, inventory monitoring, authentication and **One Nation One Ration Card** portability—supported food assistance for **800 million-plus** people during the pandemic. Digital access must include exception handling so biometric/connectivity failures do not exclude eligible households.
- Shift from staple calories toward affordable **pulses, fruit, vegetables and suitable animal-source foods**; strengthen **PM POSHAN, Anganwadi/ICDS services, women-led enterprises and FPOs**. Connect AgriStack, e-NAM and geospatial planning with physical storage/cold chains and inclusive access.
- Source's “60%+ cannot afford a healthy diet” lacks a clear matching survey year and is **not accepted as a 2024 estimate**; retain the affordability challenge without mixing older series. Similarly, “13% farm-to-market loss” is an approximate food-loss statistic, not a verified India-specific loss for this issue.
- Calorie sufficiency can coexist with micronutrient deficiency and obesity. Evaluate coverage, dietary diversity, affordability, resilience and exclusion, rather than treating digitisation or output growth alone as proof of SDG 2 success by 2030.

topics.title: Semaglutide and GLP-1 receptor agonists
topics.subject: Science and Technology
topics.markdown:
## Mechanism and significance
- **Semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist**, mimicking an incretin hormone. It increases **glucose-dependent insulin secretion**, reduces glucagon secretion, delays gastric emptying and influences appetite/satiety.
- Mechanism: GLP-1 receptor activation → greater insulin response when glucose is elevated + less hepatic glucose output + reduced appetite → improved glycaemic control and weight reduction.
- Evidence supports glucose control, weight-management benefits and reduction of cardiovascular or renal risk in specified patient groups. Benefits and eligibility depend on indication, formulation and trial population; an average “4 kg loss” is not a universal outcome.
## Milestones and a correction
- **Ozempic: US FDA approval for type 2 diabetes in 2017**; **Wegovy: approval for chronic weight management in 2021**, alongside diet and activity. Brand/formulation indications should not be assumed interchangeable. [FDA](https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USFDA/bulletins/2e2adc7).
- **Later development — 5 September 2025:** WHO added semaglutide and other GLP-1 therapies to its Essential Medicines List for specified adults with type 2 diabetes and relevant cardiovascular/renal disease and obesity. The source's **“WHO EML in 2023” is incorrect**; this had not happened by the April article date. EML inclusion guides national selection and procurement, not automatic free supply or approval for every use. [WHO](https://www.who.int/news/item/05-09-2025-who-updates-list-of-essential-medicines-to-include-key-cancer--diabetes-treatments).
## Access and safety
- Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and constipation. Important warnings include pancreatitis and gallbladder problems; dehydration can affect kidney function. Hypoglycaemia risk is generally lower than with insulin alone but **not zero**, particularly with insulin/sulfonylureas. [FDA safety information](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/human-drug-compounding/fda-alerts-health-care-providers-compounders-and-patients-dosing-errors-associated-compounded).
- High cost, uneven access, supply quality and long-term adherence matter. Clinical follow-up and nutrition/activity remain important; medicine does not replace prevention or equitable primary care.
- UPSC angle: India’s combined diabetes-obesity burden, NCD expenditure, essential-medicine policy, affordability, generic competition and **SDG 3**.

## June 2025: compare tirzepatide
- **Tirzepatide activates both GIP and GLP-1 receptors**; semaglutide activates **GLP-1** receptors. Both are synthetic peptide medicines; incretin signalling links intestinal hormones to glucose regulation and satiety. [FDA tirzepatide overview](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-new-medication-chronic-weight-management).
- Source describes injections, but semaglutide also has an **oral formulation**; brand, route, indication and approval jurisdiction must be distinguished. Access, affordability, regulated supply and continuing clinical care matter to public-health policy; drug effects are not a substitute for population-level prevention.
- Source's broad BMI thresholds are indication-specific eligibility descriptions, not personalised treatment rules. Its undifferentiated obesity count/diabetes rank should not be learned without survey/year definitions.
- Adjacent PYQ recall: **ACE2 → spread of viral diseases (2021, d); Bollgard I/II → GM crops (2022, b); B and T cells → protection against pathogens (2022, d)**. These are separate biotechnology/immunology concepts, not mechanisms of the two medicines.

## June 28 graphic: formulations and statistics
- Source infographic explicitly shows **oral semaglutide (Rybelsus)**: semaglutide is **not exclusively injectable**. It quotes old 10-tablet pack prices **₹3,170/₹3,520/₹3,870 for 3/7/14 mg**; these are the clipping's dated retail examples, not current prices, interchangeable dosing or treatment costs.
- Graphic's **10.13 crore diabetes estimate** needs cohort/year context. NFHS-5 **24% women/23% men** corresponds to **overweight or obesity (BMI ≥25)** in the surveyed age groups, not obesity alone. The body's “135 million obese /India second in diabetes” claims do not establish comparable age-standardised 2025 prevalence rankings.
- Existing tirzepatide **dual GIP/GLP-1** versus semaglutide **GLP-1** distinction, prescription eligibility, GI side effects and affordability cover the repeated text. **BMI ≥30 or ≥27 plus relevant comorbidity** are common weight-management label thresholds, not permission for unsupervised use or identical criteria for every Indian patient.
- Ancillary PYQ recall: **ACE2 (2021)—viral diseases; Bollgard (2022)—GM crops; B/T cells (2022)—protection from pathogens**. The source's practice question is not a PYQ.

topics.title: Diabetes: types, complications and public health response
topics.subject: Science and Technology
topics.markdown:
## Core distinction
- **Diabetes mellitus:** chronic hyperglycaemia due to inadequate insulin production, impaired insulin action, or both. Insulin is produced by pancreatic **beta cells** and helps regulate glucose uptake/storage.
| Type | Main feature | Revision trap |
|---|---|---|
| Type 1 | Usually autoimmune beta-cell destruction; insulin deficiency | Can begin in adults as well as children; education does not prevent autoimmune onset |
| Type 2 | Insulin resistance with inadequate compensatory insulin secretion | Genetics and social/environmental conditions interact with obesity/inactivity; children can develop it |
| Gestational | Hyperglycaemia arising during pregnancy | Requires pregnancy-specific screening and follow-up; mother and child have higher future type 2 risk |
- **Type 1 requires insulin**; type 2 may require lifestyle support, medicines and sometimes insulin. Type 2 is the large majority of cases; hospital-specific “2% type 1” is not a national population prevalence estimate. [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/diabetes).
## Complications and early recognition
- Persistent hyperglycaemia → vascular/nerve damage → **retinopathy, kidney disease, neuropathy, foot ulcers/amputation, heart disease and stroke**. Thirst, frequent urination, fatigue and unexplained weight loss may occur; type 2 can remain unrecognised for years.
- Family history and HLA associations such as **DR3-DQ2 / DR4-DQ8** indicate susceptibility, not inevitable disease. The source’s fixed “8% family risk” and undated child counts should not be treated as universal estimates.
## Diagnosis versus monitoring
- Laboratory tests include fasting plasma glucose, **HbA1c** and oral glucose tolerance testing. HbA1c reflects approximately three months’ average glycaemia; diagnostic selection differs for pregnancy/type 1 and some blood disorders.
- Typical **non-pregnant adult** diabetes thresholds: **HbA1c ≥6.5%; fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL; two-hour OGTT ≥200 mg/dL**. Confirmation is usually required unless there is unequivocal symptomatic hyperglycaemia; pregnancy uses different criteria. [NIDDK](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/tests-diagnosis?dkrd=www2.niddk.nih.gov).
- Glucose meters/CGMs support monitoring; closed-loop **“artificial pancreas”** systems link sensors and insulin delivery, rather than replacing the anatomical pancreas. Clinical interpretation and follow-up remain necessary.
## Public health response
- **NPCDCS launched in 2010**, now broadened as **NP-NCD**: health promotion, screening, primary-care management, district/CHC capacity, referral and follow-up. [NHM](https://nhm.gov.in/nhm/index1.php?lang=1&level=2&lid=604&sublinkid=1048).
- **WHO Global Diabetes Compact launched in 2021**, insulin discovery’s centenary: affordable medicines/technologies, primary-care integration, prevention and equitable care. **World Diabetes Day: 14 November**, Banting’s birthday; “Access to Diabetes Education” was the **2022 theme**, not a permanent theme. [WHO Compact](https://www.who.int/initiatives/the-who-global-diabetes-compact).
- Strengthen longitudinal NCD care at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, affordable insulin/medicines and testing, nutrition/activity support, tobacco control and maternal screening; telemedicine can complement local services. Health education can reduce type 2 risk and complications, not prevent all childhood/type 1 diabetes.
- Epidemiological numbers depend on year, age coverage and method. The source’s “77 million, IDF 2021” attribution is unreliable; avoid presenting it as India’s current total or an official “diabetes capital” ranking.

topics.title: CORLEO and hydrogen-powered robotic mobility
topics.subject: Science and Technology
topics.markdown:
## CORLEO: concept, not an operational fleet

- **3 April 2025:** Kawasaki announced CORLEO, a **2050 concept** for Expo 2025 Osaka–Kansai, opening on 13 April. Promotional terrain footage does not establish commercial availability or independently tested field performance.
- Four-legged personal off-road mobility concept combines motorcycle and robotics design; independently moving rear legs absorb shocks, while rider weight shifts guide movement.
- Proposed energy chain: **hydrogen canister → hydrogen engine → electricity → robotic leg movement**. The manufacturer specifies an **engine**, not a hydrogen fuel cell. [Kawasaki announcement](https://global.kawasaki.com/en/corp/newsroom/news/detail/?f=20250403_9193)
- Robotic assistance and human–machine interfaces could support difficult-terrain exploration, rescue and logistics; these are potential applications, not demonstrated deployments of CORLEO.

## Revision distinctions

| Hydrogen engine | Hydrogen fuel cell |
|---|---|
| Burns hydrogen to produce mechanical power; a generator can supply electricity | Electrochemical conversion directly produces electricity |
| Combustion can produce nitrogen oxides | No combustion within the cell |

Hydrogen's climate benefit depends on its production, storage and transport. No carbon in the fuel does **not** mean zero lifecycle emissions. Safety, fuel infrastructure, reliability, affordability and environmental disturbance remain implementation questions.

topics.title: Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana
topics.subject: Governance in India
topics.markdown:
## Clean cooking access

- **PMUY launched in May 2016**, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas: deposit-free LPG connections in adult women's names for eligible poor households without an existing household LPG connection.
- Initial target: **5 crore connections**, subsequently expanded to **8 crore**. Inclusion extended beyond the original deprivation-based coverage to SC/ST households, PMAY-Gramin and Antyodaya beneficiaries, forest dwellers, most backward classes, tea/ex-tea garden communities and island residents.
- Connection support covers cylinder security deposit, regulator, hose and installation. The initial assistance for a 14.2-kg connection was **₹1,600**; do not treat this historical amount as an unchanging entitlement.
- **Ujjwala 2.0, August 2021:** additional connections, free first refill and stove; migrants can use prescribed self-declarations for address and family composition instead of conventional address/ration-card documents. [PIB Ujjwala 2.0 overview](https://static.pib.gov.in/WriteReadData/specificdocs/documents/2022/mar/doc202232832001.pdf)

## Access must become sustained use

**Connection → affordable refill → reliable delivery → regular clean cooking → lower smoke exposure.** A connection count measures access, not exclusive LPG use or verified health gains.

- Benefits: reduced biomass collection, women's drudgery and household smoke exposure; time for education and income generation.
- Barriers: refill cost and irregular income, delivery distance, continued biomass use alongside LPG, inadequate awareness and safety support.
- Priorities: targeted refill assistance through DBT, dependable last-mile distribution, smaller-cylinder options, LPG Panchayats, refill-based monitoring and locally suitable clean alternatives such as biogas.
- **Exam trap:** a free first refill does not mean unlimited free refills. Subsidies are separate, periodically revised policy benefits. [Official eligibility and benefits](https://www.pmuy.gov.in/faq.html)

topics.title: LPG pricing and household affordability
topics.subject: Indian Economy
topics.markdown:
## How the cost builds up

**International LPG benchmark → import/landed cost → rupee conversion → domestic distribution and taxes → retail price → eligible DBT → effective household cost.**

- LPG consists mainly of **propane and butane**, liquefied under pressure; CNG is predominantly methane stored as compressed gas. LPG chiefly serves cooking/heating; CNG commonly serves transport. Both are fossil fuels unless produced through alternative pathways.
- Import-parity pricing represents equivalent imported supply cost: overseas price, ocean freight, insurance/port-related charges and applicable duties. Saudi Aramco's **Contract Price (Saudi CP)** is an important benchmark.
- Rupee depreciation raises the rupee cost of dollar-priced imports, other things equal; appreciation has the opposite effect.
- Bottling, domestic freight, marketing, distributor commission and applicable taxes affect delivered cost and location-wise differences.

## Price is not the same as cost

- International costs influence domestic supply economics, but **domestic cooking-cylinder retail prices are modulated by government policy**. They do not automatically change every month with the benchmark.
- Commercial and domestic cylinders have different pricing patterns; do not infer one from the other.
- PMUY's targeted **DBT refill support** reduces the eligible consumer's effective cost. This differs from an OMC's **under-recovery**—the gap between supply cost and realised regulated price.
- **February 2025 example:** government reported rising Saudi CP alongside a reduction in effective PMUY prices since August 2023, illustrating incomplete pass-through. These are dated comparisons, not today's cylinder price. [PIB parliamentary reply](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2118208&lang=1&reg=37)

**Policy trade-off:** protect clean-cooking affordability while controlling fiscal cost, targeting benefits and limiting prolonged financial stress on oil marketing companies.

topics.title: Ecocide and environmental criminal accountability
topics.subject: Environment
topics.markdown:
## Proposed international crime

- **Ecocide** denotes exceptionally grave environmental destruction. A 2021 independent expert-panel proposal covers unlawful or recklessly disproportionate acts knowingly risking severe damage that is widespread or long-lasting; this is a **proposed definition**, not an enacted universal offence.
- Campaigners seek its addition as a **fifth Rome Statute crime**. The ICC presently covers **genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression**; ecocide has not become a separate ICC crime. [ICC Rome Statute](https://www.icc-cpi.int/publications/core-legal-texts/rome-statute-international-criminal-court)
- The ICC prosecutes **natural persons**, subject to jurisdiction and admissibility rules—not states or companies as entities. Domestic law may separately provide corporate liability.
- **Belgium adopted a revised criminal code in 2024**, including ecocide. Adoption and commencement differ; its new code entered into force in **September 2026**, a later development. Belgium's legislation did not itself amend the Rome Statute. Avoid the claim that it was the first European country ever to criminalise environmental destruction. [Belgian Justice: code reform](https://www.justice.belgium.be/fr/themes/securite_et_criminalite/reforme_du_code_penal)

## India: existing protection, distinct-offence debate

| Framework | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 | Umbrella environmental protection |
| Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, amended in 2022 | Species/habitat protection and regulated wildlife trade |
| Forest conservation legislation, 1980, amended/renamed in 2023 | Regulation of diversion of covered forest land |
| Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016 | Management of compensatory-afforestation funds |

The supplied April 2025 discussion proposes a distinct ecocide offence; existing environmental violations can already attract legal consequences. A new offence must specify severity, geographical/duration thresholds, culpability and evidentiary standards.

**Case for:** ecological justice, deterrence, polluter accountability and stronger protection against major ecosystem damage. **Challenges:** causation across actors, enforcement capacity, fair development decisions and avoiding vague criminalisation. Clear thresholds, independent ecological evidence and accountable enforcement matter as much as a new label.

topics.title: MASLD and metabolic liver disease
topics.subject: Science and Technology
topics.markdown:
## Terminology and mechanism

- **MASLD:** metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. The 2023 nomenclature uses **liver steatosis plus at least one cardiometabolic risk factor**; it is more than simply replacing an old label in every case.
- **MASH** replaces NASH for the inflammatory form with liver-cell injury. Greater alcohol exposure alongside metabolic dysfunction has a separate **MetALD** category. [AASLD nomenclature](https://www.aasld.org/new-masld-nomenclature)
- Risk factors include excess adiposity, insulin resistance/type-2 diabetes, abnormal lipids and hypertension; genetics and other endocrine/metabolic conditions also contribute. Children and **lean people** can be affected—normal body weight does not exclude disease.

**Possible progression:** steatosis → MASH → fibrosis → cirrhosis → liver failure/cancer. Progression is **not inevitable**, and individuals differ substantially.

## Detection and care

- Complications extend beyond the liver: cardiovascular disease, diabetes-related problems and kidney disease. Early disease may be clinically silent.
- Assessment combines history, metabolic evaluation and blood tests with imaging; elastography assesses stiffness/fibrosis risk, and biopsy is reserved for selected uncertain or higher-risk cases. Normal liver enzymes do not alone exclude disease.
- Healthy diet, activity, appropriate weight management and control of associated metabolic conditions remain central; individual treatment requires clinical assessment.
- **Correction to the source:** on **14 March 2024**, the FDA approved **resmetirom (Rezdiffra)** for selected adults with **non-cirrhotic NASH and moderate-to-advanced fibrosis**, with diet/exercise, through accelerated approval. Thus “no FDA-approved treatment” was already outdated in April 2025. This is not an approval for every person with fatty liver or evidence that all disease is curable. [FDA approval](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-treatment-patients-liver-scarring-due-fatty-liver-disease)
- India integrated NAFLD into its NCD programme framework on **22 February 2021**. [PIB operational-guidelines launch](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=1699904&lang=2&reg=48) Screening/referral and sustained metabolic-risk management are more useful than treating an unverified single prevalence percentage as nationally representative.
## June 2025: lifestyle measures and source cautions
- Core MASLD/MASH definitions, risk factors, possible progression, diagnosis and **2024 FDA resmetirom approval** are already covered; PDF's “no FDA-approved medication” remains obsolete. Approval applies to selected adults with non-cirrhotic disease/moderate–advanced fibrosis, not every person with steatosis.
- Lifestyle evidence differentiates targets in adults with excess weight: **≥5% sustained loss** helps liver fat; **7–10%** improves inflammation; **≥10%** may improve fibrosis. Tailored activity preferably ** >150 min/week moderate or 75 min/week vigorous**,appropriate diet and metabolic-risk management; these are general clinical-guideline targets, not a guaranteed cure or identical prescription for every patient. [EASL–EASD–EASO 2024 guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC 11299976/).
- **PCOS, sleep apnoea, hypothyroidism, family/genetic susceptibility** can accompany metabolic risks; lean people/children may be affected. Cardiovascular and kidney/diabetes complications matter alongside liver disease.
- Ultrasound/MRI detect steatosis differently; **FibroScan elastography** chiefly supports fibrosis-risk assessment, not a stand-alone universal biopsy replacement. **ALT/AST can be normal** despite disease. Progression to cirrhosis/cancer is not inevitable; percentages/arrows in the page graphic are not individual forecasts.
- Source **“ICMR-INDIAB nearly 30% urban NAFLD”** lacks an identifiable cohort/test definition and should not be memorised as nationally representative liver-disease prevalence. INDIAB's well-known diabetes/metabolic estimates cannot automatically establish this liver statistic.
- India integrated NAFLD into the NCD programme in **2021**; Ayushman Bharat primary-care screening/referral is an implementation opportunity,not proof every centre delivers universal liver imaging. Prevent obesity/metabolic disease and strengthen follow-up rather than rely only on a prevalence slogan.

topics.title: University Grants Commission and higher-education regulation
topics.subject: Governance in India
topics.markdown:
## Evolution

**1944 Sargeant Report → 1945 University Grants Committee → 1947 wider university coverage → 1948–49 Radhakrishnan Commission → 1952 grants-referral decision → 28 December 1953 inauguration → November 1956 statutory establishment.**

The initial committee oversaw Aligarh, Banaras and Delhi universities. Maulana Abul Kalam Azad inaugurated the UGC; the **UGC Act, 1956** supplied its statutory basis. Headquarters: **New Delhi**. [UGC genesis](https://www.ugc.gov.in/Aboutus/Genesis)

## Composition and powers

- Section 5 specifies **Chairman, Vice-Chairman and ten other members**, appointed by the Central Government—**not “up to ten”**. The chairman is selected from outside serving Central/State government officers; membership includes government and academic representation.
- Coordinates university education, determines/maintains teaching, examination and research standards, distributes eligible grants and advises governments.
- University establishment and degree-awarding authority depend on law; UGC recognition is not permission for any college to declare itself a university. Under section 3, the **Central Government**, on UGC advice, declares eligible institutions deemed-to-be universities. [UGC Act](https://www.education.gov.in/sites/upload_files/mhrd/files/upload_document/ugc_act.pdf)
- **Union List entry 66** already covers coordination/determination of higher-education standards. The **42nd Amendment, 1976** moved general education to **Concurrent List entry 25**; it did not create Union authority over standards for the first time.

## Institutions and reform

| Body | Principal role |
|---|---|
| UGC | University education coordination, standards and eligible grants |
| AICTE | Technical-education planning/standards under its statutory remit |
| NAAC | Higher-education assessment/accreditation |
| NCTE | Teacher-education regulation |
| NCERT | School curriculum, research and educational support |

**NEP 2020 proposal:** Higher Education Commission of India with **NHERC** (regulation), **NAC** (accreditation), **HEGC** (grants), and **GEC** (academic standards/framework). A policy proposal is not proof that UGC has already been abolished.

Digital tools: **SWAYAM** online courses; **National Academic Depository** digital academic awards; **Academic Bank of Credits** credit accumulation/transfer. These support mobility while requiring authentic records, quality standards and institutional interoperability.
## May 2025 editorial critique
- The article argues UGC's grant-making and regulatory roles may conflict and calls for abolition; this is **a reform argument**, not proof of abolition or universally established institutional failure.
- Separate regulator, accreditation, funding and academic-standard functions with clear accountability if pursuing NEP's proposed HECI structure; institutional change requires the applicable law and implementation, not rhetoric alone.

topics.title: Governor: constitutional powers and State relations
topics.subject: Indian Polity
topics.markdown:
## Constitutional position
- **Article 153:** Governor for each State; the same person may serve multiple States. **Article 155:** appointed by the President. Constitutional head of the State and a link with the Union; the office must uphold constitutional government rather than act as a party representative.
- **Article 156:** ordinarily five years, subject to the President’s pleasure; continues until successor assumes office. Pleasure is not a licence for arbitrary removal.
- **Articles 157–158:** Indian citizen, at least 35 years; cannot remain a legislator or hold another office of profit; entitled to official residence and prescribed emoluments.
- **Article 161:** clemency for offences against laws within State executive power. **Article 163:** Council of Ministers aids/advises, except constitutionally recognised discretion. **Article 164:** appoints Chief Minister and other ministers on CM’s advice.
- **Article 200:** assent, withholding/return for reconsideration where permitted, or reservation for President; mandatory reservation applies where a Bill would derogate from High Court powers so as to endanger its constitutional position. A Money Bill cannot be returned under the first proviso.
## 8 April 2025: Tamil Nadu Bills judgment
- The Supreme Court found the Governor’s handling of ten re-enacted Tamil Nadu Bills unconstitutional and used **Article 142** to deem them assented to. Rejecting a pocket veto, it prescribed timelines; the source’s generic statement that Bills can be withheld indefinitely misses this day’s central development.
| Situation in the April judgment | Outer period |
| --- | --- |
| Withhold/reserve on ministerial advice | One month |
| Withhold contrary to advice: return with message | Three months |
| Reserve contrary to advice | Three months |
| Bill re-presented after reconsideration | Assent within one month |
- President’s decision on reserved Bills: three months, with reasons communicated for delay. These were **judicial directions in this dated judgment**, not time limits written into Article 200. [Supreme Court judgment, 8 April 2025](https://api.sci.gov.in/supremecourt/2023/45314/45314_2023_11_1501_60770_Judgement_08-Apr-2025.pdf).
## Later legal clarification: 20 November 2025
- In its Article 143 Presidential Reference opinion, the Constitution Bench rejected courts imposing universal timelines or substituting constitutional assent through “deemed assent”. Prolonged unexplained inaction can still invite limited judicial intervention requiring action. Keep this later clarification separate from the April news. [Supreme Court opinion](https://www.api.sci.gov.in/supremecourt/2025/39157/39157_2025_1_1501_66169_Judgement_20-Nov-2025.pdf).
## Friction and reform
- Disputes: inviting a party to form government, timing floor tests, delaying Bills, partisan public comments and perceived dependence on the Union for appointment/removal.
- Constitution-review and commission debates stress impartial appointments, consultation with the CM, secure tenure and restraint. **Punchhi Commission (2010)** proposed a State-legislature impeachment mechanism; it is a recommendation, not an enacted constitutional removal process. National Constitution Review Commission’s final report was **2002**, despite the source’s 2001 reference.
- Mains link: parliamentary responsibility, federalism and separation of powers require constitutional offices to facilitate elected government while protecting legitimate constitutional safeguards.
## Constitutional governance: 19 April editorial
- The April Tamil Nadu ruling illustrates **elected legislature → responsible ministry → constitutional head**, with judicial review addressing unconstitutional delay. Articles **74 and 163** provide ministerial aid and advice; constitutionally recognised discretion has limits.
- **Article 201** governs Presidential consideration of reserved State Bills; **Article 142** enables complete justice; **Article 145(3)** requires at least five judges for a substantial constitutional interpretation question. The editorial's larger-bench concern is a constitutional debate, not a finding that the April judgment was void.
- Reform proposals: clearer assent procedures, impartial gubernatorial conduct and timely reasoned decisions. Balance federal autonomy and democratic accountability with separation of powers.
- The April ruling's one-/three-month periods were **maximum limits for different situations**, not a universal minimum-one-month waiting period. Its subsequent legal position is recorded separately in this topic. [8 April judgment](https://api.sci.gov.in/supremecourt/2023/45314/45314_2023_11_1501_60770_Judgement_08-Apr-2025.pdf).

## 24 April: judicial activism and constitutional democracy
- The editorial rejects the label “judicial despotism”; this is an argument, not a judicial finding. **Activism** uses interpretation/remedies to protect rights or address governance gaps; **overreach** takes over policy choices beyond constitutional authority.
- **Articles 13, 32 and 226** underpin rights protection/judicial review; judicial review is part of the basic structure. **Article 142** empowers the Supreme Court to do complete justice in pending causes, subject to constitutional limits; it is not a general power to legislate.
- The Tamil Nadu assent judgment illustrates the tension between preventing constitutional paralysis and respecting institutional boundaries; its April directions and later clarification are recorded above.
- Examples of independence cited: electoral-bonds invalidation, NJAC invalidation and reversal of President’s Rule in Arunachal Pradesh. Judicial approval in other cases and criticism of bail/civil-liberties handling do not establish a single uniform institutional stance.
- **Correction:** the source groups CAA with measures upheld by the Supreme Court; it supplies no final CAA merits judgment establishing that proposition. Do not confuse pending challenges or interim decisions with final constitutional validation.
- Constitutional democracy protects rights, minorities and federalism alongside electoral mandates. Fair criticism, reasoned judgments, judicial restraint and visible impartiality support public trust; unelected judges’ role requires constitutional justification and accountability.

## 4 May 2025: West Bengal report
- The clipping reports Governor **C. V. Ananda Bose’s** recommendations after April Murshidabad communal violence: inquiry under the **Commissions of Inquiry Act 1952**, stronger Union intervention where State machinery fails, and BSF outposts in vulnerable areas. These are proposals, not proof they were enacted.
- He mentioned **Article 356** without presenting a formal recommendation for President’s Rule. A Governor’s report does not itself impose President’s Rule: constitutional conditions, Presidential action, parliamentary approval and judicial review apply. Ordinary law-and-order difficulty alone does not automatically establish constitutional breakdown.
- Source reports his **18–19 April visits** and public demands including a permanent BSF presence; distinguish citizens’ requests from operational deployment decisions.

## Presidential Reference: May 2025 snapshot
- **13 May 2025:** President Droupadi Murmu referred **14 questions under Article 143(1)** concerning Governor/President assent under **Articles 200–201**, discretion, judicial timelines/review, Article 142 remedies, bench composition and Centre–State jurisdiction. The April ruling and separately recorded **20 November 2025 opinion** must remain distinct chronological stages.
- **Article 143(1):** President may refer a question of law/fact which has arisen or is likely to arise and is sufficiently publicly important; Supreme Court may report an advisory opinion after hearing. **Article 143(2)** concerns disputes of the kind excluded by the proviso to Article 131, including specified pre-Constitution agreements; its text uses **shall** for the Court's report. Do not transfer the discretionary subsection-(1) wording indiscriminately to subsection (2).
- Advisory reference is not an ordinary appeal/review petition or automatic stay of an existing judgment. Opinions carry substantial constitutional authority; “non-binding” should not be read as permission to disregard authoritative constitutional interpretation.
- Source's questions **12–14** concern **Article 145(3)** Constitution Bench requirements, limits of **Article 142**, and **Article 131** original jurisdiction. Not every case mentioning the Constitution automatically requires a larger Bench; the test concerns substantial constitutional interpretation.
- The April three-month Presidential period was a **judicial direction**, not text newly inserted into Article 201. Judicial review of inaction, directions to constitutional institutions and **Article 361** personal immunity need separate analysis; “mandamus against the President personally” overstates the position.
- Examples: **Berubari reference (1960)** on territorial cession; **Keshav Singh privilege reference (1964)**, correcting PDF 1965; **Special Courts Bill (1978)**. Court declined to answer the Ayodhya historical reference (**1993 reference, 1994 opinion**) and returned the **1982 J&K resettlement reference in 2001** without an opinion. The source's simple “sub judice” explanations are not exhaustive accounts of these decisions.
- Mains: prevent legislative paralysis while respecting ministerial responsibility, separation of powers, federalism and proper judicial procedure; potential reforms/larger-Bench proceedings were possibilities at the issue date, not completed outcomes. [Primary Court record containing the reference and later analysis](https://www.api.sci.gov.in/supremecourt/2025/39157/39157_2025_1_1501_66169_Judgement_20-Nov-2025.pdf).

## Advisory jurisdiction: additional reference examples
- Reference proceeds on ministerial advice; **Article 145(3)** requires at least five judges for Article 143 reference hearings. The (1)/(2) wording and May 2025 reference are explained above.
- Additional examples: **Delhi Laws 1951** (delegated legislation); **Kerala Education Bill 1958** (rights/education); **Presidential election 1974**; **Third Judges 1998** (appointments).
- **Cauvery reference/opinion 1991**, not a blanket 1992 permission to appeal prior judgments. A reference is not an ordinary appellate/review route.
- Canada permits statutory references; US federal courts ordinarily reject advisory opinions because of case-or-controversy requirements. Advisory jurisdiction is not unique worldwide to India. [Court’s reference analysis](https://www.api.sci.gov.in/supremecourt/2025/39157/39157_2025_1_1501_66169_Judgement_20-Nov-2025.pdf).

## Comparative reference jurisdiction: practice clarification
- Canada’s federal reference power comes from **section 53 of the Supreme Court Act**, exercised by the Governor in Council; provincial references use their applicable provincial frameworks. Do not label it a directly equivalent constitutional Article or say every provincial government sends references directly to the Supreme Court. [Canadian Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/S-26/section-53.html).
- The May 25 practice sheet’s absolute “no precedential value” claim for Indian advisory opinions is misleading: Article 143 opinions have substantial constitutional authority, as the earlier discussion explains.

topics.title: India–UAE relations
topics.subject: International Relations
topics.markdown:
## Partnership trajectory
- Diplomatic relations established **1972**. The PM’s **2015** visit set the decision to elevate ties; the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership agreement was signed **January 2017**. [2017 agreement list](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=1514426&lang=2&reg=48).
- **CEPA:** signed February 2022, effective May 2022; tariff reductions, market access, services and investment cooperation. USD 100 billion was a trade-expansion target, not proof of achievement in every reporting year.
- April source describes UAE as India’s third-largest trading partner and reports roughly USD 20–21 billion investment, including USD 15.5 billion FDI. These are source-period estimates; cumulative FDI and total investment are different measures and rankings vary by financial year.
## Cooperation map
| Area | Institutions, initiatives and significance |
| --- | --- |
| Trade | CEPA supports textiles, gems/jewellery, pharmaceuticals and diversified commerce |
| Payments | UPI–AANI instant-payment linkage and RuPay–JAYWAN cooperation; local INR–AED settlement reduces transaction friction |
| Energy | Crude, LNG and LPG supply; upstream investment, strategic reserves and renewables diversify energy security |
| Defence | Joint Defence Cooperation Committee; Desert Flag air and Desert Cyclone land exercises; IDEX/NAVDEX participation |
| Education | Indian curriculum schools; IIT Delhi–Abu Dhabi campus supports higher-education internationalisation |
| Space | ISRO–UAE Space Agency cooperation for peaceful space use; research and technology links |
| People | Large Indian diaspora, worker welfare, remittances and cultural links; BAPS temple in Abu Dhabi inaugurated in 2024 |
- **Payments caution:** agreements to interlink systems do not establish universal operational availability. RBI’s July 2023 MoU covered UPI–UAE Instant Payment Platform, RuPay–UAESWITCH, and exploration of messaging-system linkage; subsequent February 2024 agreements named AANI and JAYWAN. [RBI](https://rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_PressReleaseDisplay.aspx?prid=56054), [Parliament implementation-status reply](https://sansad.in/getFile/loksabhaquestions/annex/183/AU901_eqt2zW.pdf?source=pqals).
## Regional and multilateral links
- **I2U2:** India, Israel, UAE, USA; joint investment in water, energy, transportation, space, health and food security.
- **India–France–UAE trilateral:** Indo-Pacific cooperation, maritime security, clean energy and wider strategic coordination. **BRICS:** South–South engagement; UAE joined in 2024.
- **IMEC:** proposed India–Middle East–Europe connectivity through Gulf and European partners; announced 2023. Potential alternative trade routes and transparent infrastructure are strategic motivations, but the corridor is not a completed transport network.
- Source estimates diaspora above 3.5 million and around 35% of population; treat population shares as dated estimates, not permanent ratios.
- Strategic value: energy and export diversification, secure sea lanes, diaspora protection and partnerships in a multipolar order. Constraints: regional conflict, corridor implementation, commercial viability and coordination among multiple partners.

## Earlier I2U2 proposals in the reproduced graphic
- **July 2022** graphic: UAE proposed **US$2 billion** integrated food parks in India; a **US$330 million Gujarat hybrid renewable project**, about **300 MW(200 MW wind+100 MW solar)**. These were announced investment proposals, not proof all facilities were completed byJuly 2025.
- July 31 clipping reports ministers agreeing to elevate defence ties; existing institutional, exercise, CEPA, payments, education, diaspora and connectivity notes cover the substantive background. Retain **2017** as the formal Comprehensive Strategic Partnership agreement date, despite the PDF's 2015 shorthand.
- The supplementary graphic's implication that India operates/maintains the UAE's **Barakah nuclear plant** is unsupported; a cooperation discussion or agreement does not transfer plant operation to India.

topics.title: Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana
topics.subject: Indian Economy
topics.markdown:
## Ten years of PMMY: April 2025
- Launched **8 April 2015**, PMMY brings small entrepreneurs into formal finance through collateral-free loans for non-corporate micro/small businesses. It covers non-farm activities and eligible allied agricultural activities; it is not a crop-cultivation subsidy or pension scheme.
- **MUDRA = Micro Units Development and Refinance Agency Ltd.** Supports/refinances last-mile lenders; does not directly lend to individual entrepreneurs. Loans are made by commercial banks, RRBs, small finance/cooperative banks, NBFCs and MFIs.
| Category | Loan range |
| --- | --- |
| Shishu | Up to ₹50,000 |
| Kishore | Above ₹50,000 to ₹5 lakh |
| Tarun | Above ₹5 lakh to ₹10 lakh |
| Tarun Plus | Above ₹10 lakh to ₹20 lakh; previous Tarun loan must have been successfully repaid |
- **Correction:** the original ₹10-lakh ceiling and three-category description are historical. Tarun Plus became effective **24 October 2024**, so the April 2025 scheme already had four categories; not every new borrower automatically qualifies for ₹20 lakh. [PIB anniversary account, 8 April 2025](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2119954&lang=1&reg=37).
- Inclusion focus: women, SC/ST/OBC, minority communities and new entrepreneurs. Access to credit should be assessed alongside business survival, repayment, income and jobs.
- Source cites Labour Ministry survey estimate of **1.12 crore net additional employment during 2015–2018**, including **69 lakh women (62%)**. This is an estimate for that historical survey period, not April 2025 employment creation or a count of unique current borrowers.
## PYQ reasoning
- **2016 prelims:** correct answer **(a), bringing small entrepreneurs into the formal financial system**. The alternatives concern crop-specific farm loans, pensions and funding voluntary skill-development organisations; these do not describe PMMY’s central aim.

topics.title: De-extinction and the dire wolf
topics.subject: Environment
topics.markdown:
## April 2025 announcement: claim versus demonstrated result
- On **7 April 2025**, Colossal Biosciences announced three pups—**Romulus, Remus and Khaleesi**—as “de-extincted” dire wolves. The scientifically cautious description is **gene-edited grey-wolf proxies with selected dire-wolf-like traits**, not genetic restoration of the extinct species.
- Company-reported workflow: ancient samples (approximately **13,000-year-old tooth** and **72,000-year-old skull material**) → infer genetic traits → edit grey-wolf donor cells at **20 sites in 14 genes** → nuclear transfer/embryo development → domestic-dog surrogate gestation. Target traits included size, musculature and coat appearance. [Company science account](https://colossal.com/direwolf/science/).
- The company’s claimed **99.5% genomic similarity** does not make a few edited genes sufficient to recreate an entire species. Resemblance, ancestry and reproductive compatibility are different ways of defining species; the project emphasises phenotype/function rather than identical ancestry.
- A **2021 Nature** ancient-DNA study found dire wolves to be a distinct lineage, splitting from living canids around **5.7 million years ago**; “six million” is a rounded description. Dire wolves disappeared roughly 12,000–13,000 years ago; exact extinction dating remains approximate. [Primary study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-03082-x).
## Methods and limits
| Method | What it can achieve | Main constraint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cloning | Copy a usable donor nuclear genome | Ancient fragmented DNA is not an intact living donor cell |
| Gene editing | Engineer selected traits in a living relative | Proxy retains much of living species’ genome |
| Selective/back breeding | Select ancestral-looking traits | Appearance does not recover every lost allele |
- Genetic blueprint alone cannot reproduce extinct habitats, learned behaviours, ecological relationships or every developmental effect. Proxy creation is therefore distinct from successful ecological restoration.
- Wider projects include mammoth-like traits using elephant-related research, woolly mice as trait models, and dodo/passenger-pigeon targets. **Pyrenean ibex cloning in 2003** produced a live-born animal that died shortly after birth; it did not establish a surviving population.
## Conservation and ethics
- Potential benefits: ancient-DNA research; improved reproductive/genetic tools; disease-resistance and genetic-diversity work for extant endangered species; carefully assessed restoration of ecological functions.
- Risks: donor/surrogate welfare, failed pregnancies and adverse edits; commercialisation of wildlife; unclear long-term health/behaviour; high costs and diversion from habitat protection; unintended effects if organisms are released.
- Rewilding benefits are conditional: suitable habitat, prey/resources, disease screening, local and Indigenous participation, welfare oversight, ecological risk assessment and continuing monitoring. A laboratory birth alone cannot establish conservation success.
## Practice: ethical answer framework
- **“Should We Play God? The Moral Limits of Scientific Innovation” (150 words, 15 marks)** is undated practice, not an identified UPSC PYQ.
- Balance potential human/conservation benefits against non-maleficence, animal welfare, precaution, distributive justice and opportunity costs. Propose transparent evidence, independent oversight, consent/participation and staged trials. Ethical limits should guide useful research and prevent unsupported commercial claims.

topics.title: Nilgiri tahr: montane grassland conservation
topics.subject: Environment
topics.markdown:
## Identity and distribution
| Feature | Recall |
|---|---|
| Species | **Nilgiritragus hylocrius**, also called Nilgiri ibex |
| Status | **Endangered**, IUCN; **Schedule I**, Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 |
| State animal | **Tamil Nadu** |
| Range | Endemic to the **southern Western Ghats**, in Tamil Nadu and Kerala |
| Habitat | Open **montane grasslands**, cliffs and the shola–grassland landscape; not a rainforest-canopy species |
| Male identification | Mature males develop a pale grey back patch: **saddlebacks** |

The Forest Department's Project Nilgiri Tahr material confirms its endangered status, Schedule-I protection and restricted shola–grassland range. Schedule-I protection is stringent but should not be memorised as an exception-free legal ban. [Tamil Nadu Forest Department project booklet](https://tnprojectnilgiritahr.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/Project-Nilgiri-Tahr-Print-R3.pdf).

## April 2025 development and conservation
- The issue's clipping announces a **joint Tamil Nadu–Kerala census from 24 April**. This is a survey announcement; no census result is supplied.
- Threats: grassland loss and degradation, livestock competition, invasive plants, poaching, climate change and isolated small populations vulnerable to local extinction.
- Habitat protection → invasive-plant control and grassland restoration → connected populations → coordinated monitoring across the two States.
- Key distinction: native montane grasslands are valuable habitat; indiscriminate tree planting can harm a grassland specialist. [Wildlife Institute of India assessment](https://digitalrepository.wii.gov.in/items/217085b0-299a-479b-866e-fd5293d785e5).

topics.title: Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana
topics.subject: Indian Economy
topics.markdown:
## Objectives and implementation
- Launched **2015**: converge irrigation investment at field level, expand assured irrigation (**Har Khet Ko Pani**), reduce water losses, encourage precision irrigation and coordinate water management at watershed/local scales.
- States, districts and Panchayati Raj Institutions participate in decentralised planning; convergence of funding and infrastructure with farm-level delivery is essential.

## Components and the administrative correction
| Programme | Focus / responsible department |
|---|---|
| AIBP | Complete major/medium irrigation projects; Ministry of Jal Shakti |
| HKKP | Surface minor irrigation; repair, renovation and restoration of water bodies; groundwater interventions; Department of Water Resources |
| CAD&WM | Command-area channels and water management; link created irrigation potential with its actual use |
| Watershed Development | Ridge-to-valley treatment, water harvesting, soil/moisture conservation; Department of Land Resources, Ministry of Rural Development |
| Per Drop More Crop | Drip/sprinkler irrigation and efficient farm water use; Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare |

**Correction:** the source presents PDMC as a current PMKSY component. It operated under PMKSY during **2015–16 to 2021–22**, then under **RKVY from 2022–23**. Micro-irrigation installation assistance is **55% for small/marginal farmers and 45% for others**, with possible State top-ups. [Agriculture Ministry, 12 December 2023](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=1985487&lang=2&reg=3).

Groundwater intervention must respect aquifer sustainability and programme eligibility; the source's phrase “developing groundwater sources in water-stressed areas” is not a licence to expand extraction everywhere.

## Significance, constraints and answer framework
- Reliable irrigation + efficient delivery → greater crop productivity and resilience → diversification into horticulture and improved livelihoods. Watershed works also conserve soil and recharge groundwater.
- Drip/sprinklers, fertigation and water budgeting reduce avoidable losses; benefits depend on maintenance, suitable crops and sound abstraction limits.
- Challenges: fragmented ministerial responsibilities, slow disbursement/project completion, uneven micro-irrigation adoption, farmer awareness and uncertain rainfall/water supply. Improve coordination, extension, maintenance and local water-user participation.
- The issue claims increased micro-irrigation, restored water bodies and higher productivity without a consistent dated quantitative series; treat these as reported outcomes, not verified numerical achievements.
- Practice answer: introduce irrigation and efficiency goals → explain programme roles → assess productivity, income, water and rainfed-area benefits → constraints → conclude with aquifer-aware local planning. The supplied undated question requests **250 words** but prints **150 marks**, an apparent typo requiring review; it is not an official PYQ.

topics.title: Monetary Policy Committee and policy instruments
topics.subject: Indian Economy
topics.markdown:
## MPC: statutory role
- **Section 45ZB, RBI Act 1934**, as amended in **2016**: Central Government constitutes a six-member MPC; its policy-rate decision binds RBI. Price stability is the primary objective while keeping growth in mind.
- **Three RBI members:** Governor (ex officio chair), Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, and an RBI officer nominated by the Central Board. **Three external members:** Central Government appointees with ability, integrity and expertise in economics/banking/finance/monetary policy.
- Majority voting; Governor has a casting vote on a tie. Quorum **four**, including Governor or, in the Governor's absence, the monetary-policy Deputy Governor. External members have **four-year terms without reappointment**. [Indian Economic Service: MPC](https://ies.gov.in/arthapedia/concept/monetary-policy-committee-mpc).

## Instruments: distinguish rates, reserves and operations
| Instrument | Function |
|---|---|
| Repo | Collateralised RBI lending to eligible banks; policy-rate anchor |
| SDF | Absorbs overnight liquidity **without collateral**; corridor floor |
| MSF | Overnight standing borrowing window for eligible banks; corridor ceiling |
| LAF / corridor | Framework for liquidity injection/absorption; SDF → repo → MSF |
| Reverse repo | RBI absorbs liquidity against securities; fixed reverse repo is no longer the corridor floor |
| Bank Rate | Reference rate aligned with MSF; also relevant to specified penalties |
| CRR | Required cash balances with RBI as a share of relevant liabilities |
| SLR | Required holdings of eligible liquid assets; distinct from CRR |
| OMO | Outright securities purchase injects durable liquidity; sale absorbs it |
| Main / fine-tuning operations | Variable-rate liquidity operations manage mismatches; tenor and instrument depend on RBI's operating framework |

SDF replaced fixed reverse repo as the corridor floor in **April 2022**; the source's list alone does not explain this change. [RBI annual-report chronology](https://www.rbi.org.in/scripts/AnnualReportPublications.aspx?Id=1384).

## 9 April 2025 decision
